restoration.item: Rear brakes — rotors & pads (two independent dealer reads)
restoration.detail: ⚠️ SUPERSEDES the old “likely fine” reading, which came from Express Oil flagging nothing on 7/11 — and that entry already carried the right caveat, that their checklist measures brake FLUID LEVEL, not pad thickness, so no pad number was ever on record. Two independent VW dealers now say the rears are done: Jim Ellis called rear rotors and pads in March 2025 at 73,631, and VW of Marietta called them again in August 2026 at 83,782, marked Critical. Ten thousand miles apart, same finding, and the rears were last done at Midas in 2022 around 54,844 — roughly 29,000 miles ago. Treat this as real rather than an upsell: it is the one item on the dealer estimate that two unrelated shops agree on. ⭐ WHERE IT SHOULD GO: not the quick-lube chain. The MK7 has an ELECTRONIC PARKING BRAKE, so the rear caliper pistons must be retracted with a scan tool in service mode rather than wound back by hand; the wrong tool or the wrong habit damages the caliper actuator motors, which are expensive. A VW specialist does this routinely. Eurofed holds the history and is the preferred specialist; Autobahn is the standing default for the big work. Do the brake fluid in the same visit — the system is being bled anyway, so the fluid is nearly free on labour. The dealer's own price for the rear job is a dealer-rate benchmark, not a quote to accept.

restoration.item: Brake fluid — REOPENED, the 7/11 exchange is in question
restoration.detail: ⚠️ REOPENED 2026-08-28 — this was marked done on the strength of a single receipt, and the world now disagrees with it. Express Oil billed a brake-fluid exchange on 2026-07-11 at 82,698. On 2026-08-26 at 83,782 — 46 days and 1,084 miles later — the VW of Marietta advisor called the fluid “really black,” and Paul's own look on 8/28 reads the reservoir as very dark grey to black. Brake fluid is a static hydraulic column, not a circulating one, so there is no mechanism to re-darken a freshly exchanged reservoir in six weeks; even a reservoir-only job should still look fresh. ⭐ WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN A BILLING DISPUTE: across all 21 rows of this car's service history (2021→2026, 43,101→83,782 mi) that 7/11 exchange is the ONLY brake-fluid service ever recorded — every other mention is a recommendation nobody acted on. If it did not happen, the car may still be on factory-original fluid approaching ten years, against a two-year interval. Old fluid absorbs water and its boiling point falls; the failure shows up as a soft or sinking pedal under sustained heavy braking — which is what a long descent off the mountain is. Pair that with rear pads two dealers have now called worn and both ingredients of brake fade are in the same car. NOT PROVEN: “really black” is a subjective call from someone selling a $264.99 flush, and the reservoir has not yet been sampled onto white to separate fluid colour from tank, float and shadow. DO: sample onto white; then have it done properly. Spec is DOT 4 LV (VW G 060 157), all four corners bled, not a reservoir exchange — and it rides nearly free on labour if it is done alongside the rear brakes. Detail and the Express Oil question: finding F-G in the private records.

restoration.item: Coolant — verify at next shop visit
restoration.detail: Two observations on record — no conclusion drawn. (1) 2025-09-15 @ 77,793 (Cannon Automotive, Jasper): an invoice note reads the coolant reservoir was empty prior to service and was topped off — a single-source vision read of one printed line, treated as an observation, not confirmed. (2) 2026-07-11 @ 82,698 (Express Oil): cooling system pressure-tested, no active leak found; reservoir at a safe level. Context, not a diagnosis: the water pump + thermostat assembly was already replaced once (Autohaus, Jun 2022 @ ~52,665 mi), so it's not the original plastic module — full part list is in the private service records. PLAN: no special trip and no call to chase — fold it into a visit that's already happening. Two natural moments: (a) the spare-key dealer trip — grab a free coolant-level eyeball while they do the free recall check (treat any 'recommended services' list as an upsell, not gospel); (b) better for a real read — a specialist visit at Autobahn, where they can properly check whether it's losing any (dye/pressure) and glance the brake pads at the same time. Eurofed also holds your history. On any eventual pump replacement, ask for a metal-impeller INA/OE kit. (3) 2026-02-02: Paul replaced the coolant expansion/overflow reservoir tank himself (DIY) — a suspect swapped out; predates the clean 7/11 pressure test. Not calling the loss solved, but it's a variable now on record. (4) ⚡ 2026-08-28 — THE LOSS IS ACTIVE, and two of the readings above are now unsafe to lean on. Paul topped the reservoir off roughly one to two weeks before 8/28 (a small top-off, not a refill) and sees fluid under the car, so the level is still falling and the 2/2026 tank swap did not close it. ⚠️ FIRST: the 7/11 Express Oil pressure test above is a claim from the same visit whose brake-fluid claim is now in question (finding F-G) — if it was never performed, “no active leak” was never established and an ordinary physical leak was never ruled out. ⚠️ SECOND: at the 8/26 dealer visit Paul asked about the coolant, was offered a full diagnostic at about $220, and declined it — so the absence of a coolant line on that visit's estimate is not a clean bill, they simply did not look. Fluid under the car also cuts against the worn-pressure-cap theory in the research notes, whose whole signature is a slow loss with NO puddle; that promotes a physical leak — the plastic thermostat/water-pump housing, already replaced once in 2022, or the turbo-to-head coolant pipe. STILL UNKNOWN and all free: the colour of the under-car fluid (pink/violet is coolant, clear is ordinary summer A/C condensate, brown/black would be oil and would point at the timing cover instead), what he topped off with (G13 or G12evo are both correct; generic green or orange is its own problem), and what is stamped on the cap now fitted. Cardboard under the car overnight answers the first. When it next goes in, ask by name for the CAP to be tested on a cap tester, separately from a system pressure test — that step gets skipped, and a system test cannot see a cap fault. ⭐ (5) COLOUR CONFIRMED 2026-08-28 — Paul reports the fluid under the car is PINK (not bright, looks watery, but a coolant pink). On this car that settles it rather than suggests it: she is a manual, so there is no red-pink automatic transmission fluid, and the MK7 has electric power steering, so there is no steering fluid either — nothing else aboard is that colour. So the loss is a physical liquid leak, which demotes the worn-cap theory (whose whole signature is a slow loss leaving NO puddle) and promotes, in order: the plastic thermostat and water-pump housing, already replaced once in 2022 and the part the tune works hardest; the turbo-to-head coolant pipe; and the inexpensive aftermarket expansion tank fitted in February, whose own seal is now a suspect rather than just its cap. This does NOT clear the upper timing cover flagged the same month — that is oil, and an upper-cover seep often wets the block without ever reaching the ground, so both can be true at once. Next, and free: note WHERE the puddle sits relative to the wheels and centreline, and let a drop dry — coolant leaves a sticky residue, water leaves nothing.

restoration.item: Upper timing chain cover — oil seep (dealer-flagged)
restoration.detail: NEW 2026-08-26 — VW of Marietta flagged the UPPER TIMING CHAIN COVER on the courtesy inspection at 83,782, and Paul marked it Critical on the sheet. On the EA888 Gen 3 this is the well-known upper-cover oil seep: a labour-heavy job around a cheap gasket. ⭐ WORTH HOLDING TWO THOUGHTS APART: this is an OIL leak, while the long-running open item on this car is a COOLANT loss. They are different fluids and probably different problems — but nobody has yet confirmed what the fluid under the car actually is, and brown or black on the cardboard would point here rather than at the cooling system. Get an independent read before buying the dealer's price; this is exactly the kind of job where a specialist's opinion on whether it is seeping or genuinely leaking changes whether it is worth doing now. Not urgent the way the brakes are.

restoration.item: Manual gearbox oil — low-priority check (was mis-filed as a DSG service)
restoration.detail: ⚠️ CORRECTED 2026-07-22: filed as a 'DSG service', but the GTI is a 6-speed MANUAL (Paul-confirmed) — there is no DSG. Manual gearbox oil is long-life (not a 40k/80k item), so this drops from 'overdue, don't skip' to a low-priority check. If changing it, verify the manual spec (commonly VW G 052 527 A2) and drain-and-fill at a visit that's already happening; skip the temp-controlled DSG fill entirely.

Routine oil at Paul's regular shop (Express Oil, Moreland Ave) on live coupons — and a FREE second-opinion look at the coolant leak while it's on the lift. GATE FIRST (call 404-659-6225): confirm they stock VW 502.00-approved oil (5W-40 preferred; a 502.00 5W-30 is also fine) + get the out-the-door price with $20-off — the coupon covers standard oil only and voids with customer-supplied oil, so gate on VW 502.00 (a 502.00 5W-30 is fine, 5W-40 preferred for the Stage-1 tune) — the real walk-away is a generic/dexos 5W-30 with NO 502.00 (then walk to Autobahn). If oil's a go: stack the FREE tire rotation (RTE026) + $15-off alignment (ASR026), and ask them to inspect + pressure-test the coolant leak (known EA888 failure = plastic water pump + thermostat housing). Coolant is VW G13 (pink) ONLY — if they don't stock it, inspect only, add nothing. Get any leak finding + repair estimate IN WRITING as a benchmark vs Autobahn. Coupons: $39.99 conv / $59.99 hi-mileage (YID726, thru 7/11) or $20-off (YDCD26, thru 7/31); free rotation + alignment thru 7/31. Full question list: .research/2026-07-08-gti-express-oil-coupons.md.

Done — running NGK R7437-8 racing plugs (the APR Stage-1 heat range), installed and doing well. These are one range colder than stock; the R7437-9 Eurofed used with the 2022 tune is the Stage-3 plug (over-cold here) and is now hard to find, so the -8 is the correct pick, not a compromise. NEXT CHANGE reminder: gap to 0.024" (they ship at 0.028" — close them down), torque ~25 Nm / 18 ft-lb dry (no anti-seize — NGK's plating already anti-seizes), dielectric grease in the coil boots, and change roughly every ~20k mi on the tune. Full spec + sources in .research/2026-07-14-gti-spark-plug-setup.md. ORIGIN (7/23 ingest): Jim Ellis quoted a $348 plug job on the 3/20/2025 estimate; Paul declined and ordered the 4x NGK R7437-8 himself five days later — declined-dealer-work-then-DIY, documented.

DONE — Paul has two working keys as of 2026-08-26. Ordered and prepaid at the VW of Marietta parts counter on 8/04, then cut and programmed there on 8/26 at 83,782 mi. The spec that was chased down held up: genuine Hella OEM flip-key-with-KESSY, FCC ID NBGFS12P01, VW part 5G0 959 752 BE family, 315 MHz, MQB48 transponder, HU66 blade, CR2025 battery. ⭐ THE COST LESSON worth carrying to the rest of the fleet: programming was billed SEPARATELY from the key and cost very nearly the same again — the part was not the whole price, and the 8/04 invoice gave no hint of it because it carried no labour line. All-in for one spare key was roughly double what the parts invoice implied. The dealer also priced TWO keys at intake, at exactly twice the one-key figure, so a third key later costs the same again — the per-key programming price does not scale down. Amounts and invoice numbers in the private records.

Paul does these himself (DIY) — not an Autobahn job. Engine air filter: VW OEM 5Q0 129 620 B. Cabin filter: VW OEM 5Q0 819 644 A (activated-carbon combination filter). Both are easy at-home swaps; pick them up and do them at the property.

Direct injection builds carbon on the intake valves; 80–100k is the window to inspect and walnut-blast — at ~81k you're just at the front edge, so it may well not be needed yet. Have the shop scope it and tell you how bad it is before you commit to the job.

No fixed interval; stretch usually needs action at 120–150k. A quick VCDS / OBDeleven read now gives a baseline — worth it on a tuned car. ⚠️ NOT THE SAME THING as the UPPER TIMING CHAIN COVER that VW of Marietta flagged on 2026-08-26 — see that separate item. Stretch is a chain-and-tensioner question; the cover is a sealing surface. Do not read the dealer's cover price as a remedy for stretch, and do not let the cover job be mistaken for having addressed this.
Both are common softening/failure points on tuned MK7s. Cheap to inspect while it's at this visit.

VW of Marietta quoted both front bumper vents, driver and passenger side, at the 2026-08-26 inspection. This is almost certainly the 7/21 cone strike showing through the in-place repair — washers, zip ties and tape held the panels, but the vents themselves read as damaged to a trained eye. Purely cosmetic and the most deferrable line on that estimate; it changes nothing about how she drives. Worth pricing against a body shop or a used part rather than the dealer's figure if it ever gets done.

restoration.detail: Paul traced a bulb-out warning to a dirty, loose connector on 2026-07-13, cleaned and reseated it, and taped rather than heat-shrinked it — the record already carried a recurrence-watch on that. ⚡ 2026-08-26: VW of Marietta quoted two license-plate bulbs at the inspection, which suggests the fault is back six weeks later and that the tape did not hold. restoration.item: ⭐ Spare tire carrier SWAP — the factory carrier is what is cracking the tailgate (SEQUENCING ITEM)
restoration.detail: THE ROOT CAUSE, and it gates the tailgate and the paint. She wears 33" Mickey Thompsons — oversized and overweight for the FACTORY carrier still on the truck. The factory carrier body-mounts to the passenger rear quarter and LATCHES TO THE TAILGATE, so the spare's mass works that latch point; the widely-reported failure is the latch tearing out of the tailgate plus quarter-panel warpage, and 33-35" is the size repeatedly named. Paul has already bought the replacement: a bumper-integrated swing-out carrier (the one whose hinges are apart — see the item below), which carries the tire on the bumper and takes the tailgate out of the load path entirely. ⚠️ EVIDENCE GRADE: the mechanism is OWNER-REPORTED forum consensus, corroborated across multiple threads and consistent with the cracks Paul can see on his own tailgate — it is NOT a Ford specification, and no published factory weight limit was found. Treat the mechanism as well-supported and any specific weight number as nonexistent rather than unknown. ⭐ THE SEQUENCE THAT SAVES PAYING TWICE: service the swing-out hinges (cheap, no parts) -> fit the new bumper/carrier and REMOVE the factory carrier -> only THEN decide and do the tailgate -> paint LAST. Repairing or replacing the tailgate while the factory carrier stays on re-damages the new work; and a replacement tailgate needs paint anyway, so sourcing must precede paint prep. Deciding the tailgate AFTER the load is removed is also a cheaper decision: with the carrier gone the existing cracks stop propagating, so a repair may be sufficient where a replacement would otherwise be needed. ⭐ REVERSIBILITY, and it changes the sequence again (2026-08-04): the factory carrier is BODY-MOUNTED, so removing it leaves holes in the passenger rear quarter — which means it must come off BEFORE bodywork, not merely before paint, so the holes are filled in the same pass. Filling them does NOT prevent ever refitting the factory carrier: hole positions are fixed by the body and the carrier is its own drilling template, and a welded-and-smoothed plug re-drills fine. What going back would really cost is cutting into finished paint (a rust initiation point), so the decision becomes reversible-at-a-price rather than irreversible. ⚠️ UNKNOWN UNTIL IT COMES OFF — check and photograph it then: whether the mount uses captive nuts, a WELDED reinforcement plate, or a separate loose backing plate. A welded reinforcement stays with the body and refitting is just a re-drill; a separate backing plate that gets removed during bodywork would have to be re-created, and THAT is the only thing that would make going back genuinely hard. CHEAP INSURANCE BEFORE REMOVAL: photograph both sides incl. behind the panel, measure hole positions off two fixed references (seams/edges/other factory holes, not 'X inches from the corner'), and KEEP the factory carrier and its hardware — it is both the template and what a future factory-correct buyer would want. Fill method: weld a plug and smooth it (body filler over a backer will telegraph and crack; leaving them open is maximally reversible but is a rust path and reads unfinished). Preserving optionality here is about DOCUMENTATION, not about leaving holes open.

restoration.item: Spare tire carrier — hinge service (currently apart)
restoration.detail: The rear swing-out carrier (the aftermarket one that doubles as a step) is disassembled and its hinge hardware is off. IDENTIFIED 2026-08-04: a pin-and-barrel hinge — a 1/2" pin down through flanged bushings seated in counterbored eyes, two hinges stacked, both halves WELDED (eye to the arm, clevis ears to the mount). INSPECTED: nothing worn — bores unworn, counterbores intact, no thread damage. So NO PARTS ARE NEEDED. What the parts actually are is DRY: there is no grease fitting anywhere in this design, so it ran unlubricated for decades, and dry reads as ruined without being ruined. The job is clean, grease, reassemble. ⭐ The pin is a PIVOT, not a clamp — snug it until the arm swings freely with no slop and retain with a nyloc; free rotation is the acceptance test, not a torque figure. Anti-seize the threads: with no zerks, a teardown is the only lubrication chance this hinge ever gets. Full identification trail, 17 photos and a standby parts spec (if a bushing turns out scored under the grime) are held privately with the vehicle's service records.

⚠️ STATE CORRECTED 2026-07-27 (Paul, ground truth): THE LEAK ITSELF IS FIXED. Rust remains. So of the two jobs below, (1) is DONE and only the metal repair is left — and this is what un-gates the new carpet, because laying carpet + jute over an active leak buys the same carpet twice.

Original find: small but significant rust in the bed near the tailgate where water got in (Paul flagged 2026-06-22). Textbook full-size Bronco failure: the tailgate leaks (glass sweep + failed access-panel barrier) and rots the rear bed corners. TWO jobs, order mattered: (1) ✅ fix the leak source — tailgate weatherstrip, esp. the corner pieces, + redo the access-panel barrier — or new metal just rots again; (2) ⏳ repair the metal: open it up to find the true extent, then Rung 1 (clean+convert+prime) if it's only scale, or Rung 2 (cut back + bonded 3M patch, or weld) if it's perforated. Bed floor isn't frame-structural, so a bonded-and-rustproofed patch is legit. Likely ours to handle. AWAITING Paul: photos + detail (size, gone-through?, how far the wet spread). Method in guides/bolores-bodywork-rust-dents.md.

📍 CURRENT STATE 2026-07-27 (Paul, ground truth): ALL THE INTERIOR CARPETING IS ALREADY OUT — he stripped it. The cargo floor is BARE, so the corner is fully exposed and scopeable right now. The photos he sent this session are OLD / pre-strip.

⚠️ PHOTO OBSERVATIONS — VISUAL READS, NOT VERIFIED (two pre-strip images). Bed floor confirmed body-colour red. Wheel wells + side panels still trimmed. The old covering was degraded jute/carpet remnant sitting directly in the wet corner — the moisture-trap mechanism, caught in the act. Damage appears LOCALIZED to the sill corner, very roughly 10–14" along it, with the surrounding red paint broadly intact — that intactness is the tell arguing against systemic rot. CANNOT distinguish packed debris vs surface scale vs perforation from an image; calling it from a photo is exactly the model-read-as-fact trap.

▶️ THE DISCRIMINATING TEST (the next action — this is why the status moved off `diagnosing`): scrape and wire-brush the corner clean, then TAP AND POKE IT WITH A SCREWDRIVER. Sound metal rings and resists; perforated metal gives. That one test picks the scenario below and is the input the Phase-1 walk-around needs.

💰 COST/TIME ESTIMATE (researched 2026-07-27). THREE THINGS MAKE THIS A CHEAP RUST REPAIR, and they belong up front: the bed floor is NOT frame-structural (so a bonded patch is legitimate — no welding, which is the usual cost cliff); it ends up UNDER CARPET; and the truck is being resprayed anyway (no blending or colour-match problem). Finish standard = SOUND AND SEALED, not invisible.
• A — surface scale, no perforation (the lean from the photo): ONE AFTERNOON, 3–5 hrs, $40–80 materials (flap disc/wire wheel, rust converter or phosphoric etch, epoxy primer, seam sealer). DIY, no shop.
• B — localized perforation, pinholes to ~fist-sized: DIY bonded patch = A WEEKEND, 8–12 hrs across two sessions (adhesive cure). $100–180 (18–20ga sheet, 3M panel adhesive, cutoff wheels, sealer, primer). Shop-welded ≈ $300–700 metro Atlanta — forum quotes of 2–3 hrs @ $35–45/hr are DATED; small independents here run $60–120/hr.
• C — the wet spread further than it looks: repro panels EXIST and are CHEAP (Raybuck 1980–96 Ford full-size bed floor repair section; patch panels generally $40–100) — the panel is never the cost, the LABOUR is. Shop cut-and-weld $800–2,000. The ~$2,500 figure that floats around forums is comprehensive floor replacement, not a corner.

MOST LIKELY: A, possibly a small B — an afternoon to a weekend, $50–180, no shop. ⚠️ CAVEAT, and it's Paul's own rule already in guides/bolores-bodywork-rust-dents.md: A BUBBLE IS THE TIP, NOT THE EXTENT — scope AFTER grinding back to clean metal, never off the surface. And the real cost of guessing wrong here is CALENDAR, not dollars: this is Phase 1, and Phase 1 gates the whole repaint. ⛔ SEQUENCING GATE (2026-08-04): the FACTORY spare tire carrier must come off and the bumper-integrated carrier go on BEFORE this — it is what is cracking the tailgate, so doing this first means re-damaging finished work. See the '⭐ Spare tire carrier SWAP' item.

Supersedes the old 'failing clear coat' plan — instead of correcting the clear coat, doing a full refinish. Larry cleans, preps and primes at his place; his buddy's shop sprays. Scope locked (2026-06-22): exterior + interior together — matching a fresh body to a tired interior would mean redoing it, so converging is better for value and means only one teardown. Colors: original factory two-tone — Scarlet Red 2D (upper) over Light Chestnut 9T (lower), per the paint block below; staying factory protects resale value. Interior panels sprayed a fresh, consistent chestnut — this also removes the hard 'match a faded panel' problem from the door-panel repair. Hand the shop the door cert-label codes, or confirm they spectro-scan off the truck. Gated on the bodywork scope (Phase 1). No deadline — paint lands after all the teardown-window work is done. Full sequence in guides/bolores-door-panel-repair.md.

SCOPE CLARIFIED 2026-07-27 (Paul): the BED STAYS BODY-COLOUR — it's currently the same Scarlet Red (2D) as the exterior upper and he wants to keep it that way. Interior PLASTIC TRIM PANELS get the chestnut. So the bed is a SHOW SURFACE in the shop's spray scope, which settles that its rust repair is squarely Phase-1 pre-paint.

WHO SPRAYS WHAT — the split that actually governs sequencing (it is NOT "before paint vs after paint"):
• THE SHOP sprays: bed (Scarlet Red 2D), wheel arches, dents, outer door skins, jambs, interior trim panels (chestnut). Every one of those gets stripped/ground/treated/filled/primed in PHASE 1, before the truck goes. All of it.
• NOBODY sprays: door cavity interiors, the floor pan under the carpet, inside the rockers. Not in a repaint's scope — no one paints inside a door shell. That's why their timing floats free; they don't skip prep, they're just not the shop's job.

⚠️ OPEN QUESTIONS FOR LARRY (each gates a real decision elsewhere) — full list in guides/bolores-shop-shortlist.md: (1) doors to bare metal or scuff-and-spray? — decides whether the door-cavity work happens before or after paint; (2) is the FRONT FLOOR PAN in scope, and if not, can he shoot it while the interior's already stripped? (cheap add, hands back cured metal to deaden onto and settles the cure gate); (3) confirm the bed in body-colour Scarlet Red 2D and what finish survives being walked on; (4) trim panels sprayed off the truck?; (5) how long is she with you? — that sizes the panel-off window.

✅ SCOPE LOCKED 2026-07-27 (Paul, correcting an agent misread the same day) — IT IS A FULL RESPRAY OF EVERYTHING IN THE FACTORY COLOURS. All body metal, THE BED INCLUDED, gets a fresh coat matching the factory colour as closely as possible after the repairs; all plastic trim gets the chestnut. THE BED IS ON THE SPRAY LIST.

*What went wrong, so it isn't re-derived:* Paul said the bed is "a factory paint job" and that he wanted to "recover" it. That was read as PRESERVE THE ORIGINAL PAINT FILM — mask the bed, don't spray it — and briefly went into this record as a 🚨 DO-NOT-SPRAY instruction, which was wrong and has been removed rather than layered over. He meant the factory COLOUR, resprayed fresh, and "re-cover" = put the carpet back over it. No preservation constraint exists.

Two things fall out of the correct reading: (1) the tailgate-corner rust patch needs no special reduced spec — it's prepped like any other body repair and sprayed in the same pass as the rest of the bed, so there's nothing to negotiate; (2) colour match on the bed is trivially guaranteed, because it's the same Scarlet Red 2D mix going on in the same session as the exterior upper — the cert-label-codes / spectro-scan question above only governs getting the mix right in the first place. ⛔ SEQUENCING GATE (2026-08-04): the FACTORY spare tire carrier must come off and the bumper-integrated carrier go on BEFORE this — it is what is cracking the tailgate, so doing this first means re-damaging finished work. See the '⭐ Spare tire carrier SWAP' item.

⛔ INTERIOR-TRIM COLOUR GATE (2026-08-05): before the shop sprays a single trim panel, the '⭐ Colour spray-out test' item must have passed — a cured SEM 4168 card judged in daylight against the leather seats. The exterior half of this job is NOT gated by it (the exterior codes are read off the cert label and are not in question); only the chestnut trim is.

⚠️ COLOUR NAME CORRECTED THROUGHOUT THIS ITEM, 2026-08-09. Every instance above said "CABERNET RED." It is SCARLET RED, code 2D, mix 6236. The paint block established this on 2026-08-04 by reading the door Vehicle Certification Label — but the fix was applied to the paint block ONLY, and four stale reads survived here plus two more in 'Soundproofing', for five days. THIS IS THE DANGEROUS ONE OF THE TWO: Medium Cabernet Red is a REAL 1989 Ford colour (code 2H / 6156) that the factory brochure lists separately from Scarlet Red, so a shop handed this item would have mixed a real, wrong, plausible-looking paint — and the item a shop actually reads is the JOB item, not the paint block. ⭐ THE LESSON, and it is the same one the Motor 2B / "Liberty" correction taught on the audio item the same day: WHEN A FACT IS CORRECTED, GREP THE WHOLE RECORD FOR THE OLD VALUE. Correcting the authoritative block and stopping there leaves the old value living in exactly the places people act from.

⭐⭐ INTERIOR SHEET METAL GOES BODY-COLOUR — PAUL'S CALL 2026-08-09, and it CLOSES OPEN QUESTION (2) ABOVE. His framing: "if it's gonna be OG and really true to itself the inside paint should match the outside paint." Correct, and it is a genuinely NEW decision — not the same as the trim-panel chestnut already locked. SCOPE: the cab FLOOR PAN, inner cab structure and kick areas get SCARLET RED 2D, in Larry's scope, sprayed while the interior is stripped.
WHY IT IS RIGHT: (1) it is FACTORY-CORRECT — Ford painted the shell before trim went in, and the pre-strip photos already confirm the BED floor is body-colour red on this truck, so Ford did exactly that here. ▶️ ONE-MINUTE GROUND-TRUTH CHECK, and it is free because the carpet is already out: LOOK AT THE CAB FLOOR. Body-colour red under there confirms it; anything else means re-scope. Do not skip this — it is an observation, not an assumption, and it costs nothing. (2) It DISSOLVES the deadening-prep problem: butyl onto fresh cured epoxy/sealer is the ideal substrate, replacing 'clean 37-year-old contaminated metal well enough.' (3) The marginal cost is the shop's MASKING TIME, not a new phase — the access is already bought by the trim spray. (4) It is the only window that will ever exist.
⛔ THREE HARD LIMITS. (a) THIS IS NOT BODY-OFF. Body off the frame is a different project by an order of magnitude. Interior gutted, glass stays, body stays on frame. (b) THE CURE GATE BECOMES REAL AND NOW GOVERNS PHASE 4 — fresh paint outgasses and butyl laid over it lifts later. The Soundproofing item already calls the gate 'free' because the truck is apart anyway; that is true but it must now be ENFORCED: ~30 days air-dry on a floor, or ask Larry to force-cure. (c) DO NOT EXTEND THIS TO DOOR CAVITIES OR ROCKER INSIDES. Nobody paints inside a door shell and it would not last; those get CAVITY WAX, which the Soundproofing item already has right — and the order matters, deaden first, wax after.

Actuator already replaced with no fix, so the signal isn't reaching it. Next: meter power switch → actuator. Prime suspect is the door-jamb boot wiring (flexes and cracks inside the rubber boot where you can't see it); also check the switch and its ground. (Refinish sequence — Phase 2: the door teardown. Do it in one door-open session alongside the panel repair, the handle-mount check, and door sound-deadening.) TIMELINE: the driver-side actuator was replaced ~Jan 2026 (no fix), and a further attempt fitting a new motor to the actuator ran ~Feb 2026 — STILL no response, so it's not the actuator, it's upstream. Confirms the wiring diagnosis (door-jamb boot wiring the prime suspect). Paul has been deferring the wire-metering step; that's the next move (last hands-on ~Feb 2026). NOTE 2026-07-22: a NEW TRQ door-lock actuator (eBay, 11/3/25) is ON-SHELF, not installed (Paul-confirmed) — reconcile against the 'actuator already replaced' note above at the next door session (two units, or a misremembered sequence).

2026-07-27: the metering is Stage-1 teardown work — it has NO paint dependency, so do it the day the panels come off rather than waiting on the shop. See guides/bolores-door-panel-repair.md STEP 6. Reconcile the on-shelf TRQ actuator against the 'already replaced' note in the same session.

🛒 LMC FD.88 catalog (2026 Vol. 2; prices expired 8/3/26 — approximate): if the metering points at the parts rather than the boot wiring — DOOR LOCK ACTUATOR part 50-7793, application 9/88–91 ($34.95; her 10/88 build date is inside the window), and POWER DOOR LOCK SWITCH part 47-0623, application 87–11/90 ($22.95). Reconcile against the on-shelf TRQ actuator before buying another.

Cruise is inoperative — no response from the steering-wheel buttons. The servo hardware and the dual-cable throttle linkage are both present, but the servo's vacuum hoses are disconnected/misrouted. Plan: reconnect the vacuum supply + vent lines and cap any open ports, inspect the old hoses for cracks, and test the servo diaphragm for vacuum hold (the common internal-leak failure) before reassembly. If it still won't engage after that, work the electrical side — the brake (BOO) switch, the speed signal (VSS), the steering-wheel switch pod, and the cruise amplifier/module behind the glove box, and confirm the 3-pin cruise connector is seated. A dig-in-when-you're-under-the-dash job; pairs naturally with the Phase-2 dash/steering-column work.

🛒 LMC FD.88 catalog (2026 Vol. 2; prices expired 8/3/26 — approximate): if the electrical side lands on the switch pod — CRUISE CONTROL SWITCH part 47-0627, application 87-91, $84.95 (catalog p.114).

Cracked through with broken clip mounts. Plan is repair-in-place, not replace: back-reinforce the cracks with heat-formed ABS sheet, rebuild the broken clip pockets from ABS, then flexible-fill the show face (3M EZ Sand 35887 — verified the right product, sold on Amazon too) and SAND TO PRIMER-READY. No more self color-matching — the paint shop sprays the chestnut as part of the interior refinish, which kills the hardest part of this job. Full materials list + step-by-step at guides/bolores-door-panel-repair.md. Gate: confirm the panel's plastic type (ABS vs PP) before buying adhesives. Phase-2 door teardown — done together with the lock, the handle-mount check, and door deadening. Still gates the audio build — a loose panel rattles and ruins subs. Fallback if the repair doesn't hold: source an '87–91 Bronco/F-series chestnut panel (long lead). PARTS (DIY, installed): new door-trim panel retainer clips = Icyhaws (Ford F150/Bronco) — fitted to rebuild the broken clip pockets.

ONE-REMOVAL PROTOCOL added 2026-07-27 → guides/bolores-door-panel-repair.md STEP 6. Paul's constraint: every on/off cycle risks cracking 37-year-old plastic. The count turns out to be FORCED and better than it feels — the panel must be off for the chestnut spray, so any install before paint is a wasted cycle by definition. Optimum is 1 REMOVAL + 1 INSTALL with the panel simply STAYING OFF in between (bench → shop → reassembly). Not a big-bang weekend: a two-day teardown then months of unhurried access. The risk is closing the window early. Guide carries the what-forces-a-second-cycle list (reused clips, buttoning up before testing, skipping age-based parts, un-run wire, doing only one door) and the removal technique — WORK WARM, pry AT each clip never between, treat clips as consumable and the panel as the thing being protected.

🛒 LMC FD.88 catalog (2026 Vol. 2; prices expired 8/3/26 — approximate): the fallback repro panel is a current LMC product, which beats hunting a used chestnut panel — DOOR PANEL SET W/POWER (windows & locks) 87-91, part 49-5582-SD Saddle ($399.95/set + $20 oversize; also -BL/-LL/-LG/-DG/-DR). Small stuff for the repair path: FASTENER REMOVAL TOOL 38-1238-F $6.24; RETAINER-DOOR PANEL 40-0793 $1.85 ea.

⭐ RESEQUENCED 2026-08-28 (paul-decided): do NOT wait on the booth. Restore both panels and REINSTALL them, accepting a second removal when paint finally happens — STEP 6's one-removal optimum was arithmetic resting on 'the booth is near-term', and that premise is gone. Consequence that changes the work: 'stop at primer-ready' only worked bench→booth with no stop, so the job now SPLITS BY SIDE OF THE PANEL — back-side structural work (cracks, bracket, clip pockets, CCF) NOW because that is the rattle fix; show-face filler and colour DEFERRED to the booth. Also moved earlier: the water shield must be RESEALED/FABRICATED before a panel goes back on, or water reaches the cabin. ⚠️ CORRECTION: STEP 1 told Paul to BUY the welder, mesh, heat gun and flexible filler for two months while all of it sat on his shelf (bought 2026-06-17→06-22, in no record until the 2026-08-28 sweep). Check .private/service-records/TOOLS.md before buying anything for this job.

NEW FRONT 2026-08-28 — the record had only the driver side until now. Panel is OFF and on the bench. In MATERIALLY BETTER SHAPE than the driver's: retainer clips still seated in their pockets, so this may be strip-clean-reinforce rather than a structural rebuild. Open work: back-side crack reinforcement (Paul confirms damage + small cracks), the DPPRK87 bracket at the torn screw hole, 1/8" CCF on the panel back, and a FABRICATED water shield — the door has none. Show-face filler and paint are DEFERRED to the booth window per the 8/28 resequence. ✅ Tooling is fully on shelf (ATOLS plastic welder, stainless mesh, welding tips, heat gun, 3M EZ Sand 05887, JB Weld) — see .private/service-records/TOOLS.md. Because MESH-WELDING IS MECHANICAL, the STEP 0 ABS-vs-PP substrate gate does NOT block this repair. Full method: guides/bolores-door-panel-repair.md STEP 7. restoration.item: Door water shields — BOTH doors have none
restoration.detail: FOUND 2026-08-28 (Paul-confirmed from the panel-off photos): there is NO vapor barrier / water shield on the door at all — the inner-skin access holes open straight into the cabin. A door is DESIGNED to let water in (it runs down the outside of the glass, past the window sweep, into the hollow, and out the drains); the shield is the only thing separating that wet side from the dry side, and the trim panel does no sealing whatever. With none fitted, rain has been reaching the back of the trim panel and the carpet — which also explains the sodden cotton pad found on the passenger panel the same day. Likely lost during the Feb-2026 Kappa speaker install and never replaced. FABRICATE, don't reseal — there is no old shield to use as a template, and none is needed: lay the sheet over the door, mark round the hole zone, cut oversize, bed it on butyl. ⚠️ SEAL TOP AND SIDES, LAP THE BOTTOM — seal it all the way round and you have built a bag that holds water against the door. Do BOTH doors, and CHECK THE DRAINS RUN CLEAR from below in the same session — that access exists only while the panel is off. PARTS ORDERED 2026-08-28: Frost King P1025B/6 6-mil black poly sheeting + LLPT 1" black butyl seal tape. Non-optional before any panel goes back on under the 8/28 resequence.

Check first: does either INSIDE door handle feel loose/floppy or fail to pull the latch? On '80–'97 OBS Fords the sheet metal behind the inside handle fatigues and cracks — the classic 'roll the window down to get out' failure. If present (likely on an '89), the proven fix is a 14-ga steel reinforcement plate that rivets onto the inner door metal — no welding, rivets included; strong forum track record (Solo Motorsports / OBS Solutions / Bronco Graveyard, also generic on eBay/Amazon). Sold as a driver+passenger pair, so do both doors while they're open in Phase 2. Adds zero extra teardown.

2026-07-27: same Stage-1 survey — check BOTH handles the day the panels come off, then order off what you find. Part of the one-removal protocol (guides/bolores-door-panel-repair.md STEP 6).

Small tear in the dash pad's vinyl/leather — Paul wants it repaired. Full step-by-step (clean → trim → sub-patch → thin-layer flexible compound → grain-set → color) in guides/bolores-dash-vinyl-repair.md. Color converges with the interior refinish: repair the substrate now, let the chestnut spray/dye pass color it with the rest. Grain-matching is the make-or-break for invisibility; use FLEXIBLE compound (the dash flexes + bakes) never rigid filler. OPEN QUESTION: is the dash pad going to the booth, getting dyed in place, or capped? Decide with the interior piece-list. (If the pad turns out cracked across a large area, the durable fix is a dash cap, not many small repairs.)

 4. LMC STOCKS ONE COLOUR PER FAMILY — Black, Blue, Gray, Red, Saddle — out of Acme's 18, and its single warm-family pick carries exactly Acme's name for 1755.

Those do not reconcile. CONSEQUENCE: 'it is an Acme board' does NOT by itself pin a colour code — you must also be in the right FABRIC LINE. LMC being foam-backed puts it in the same line as 1755, which is why this is a caution and not a refutation.
ALSO: **NO PUBLISHED CROSS-REFERENCE EXISTS ANYWHERE** — not on LMC, not in any catalog, and ⭐ ACME'S OWN SITE DOES NOT EVEN LIST THE 81-96 BRONCO ABS BOARD (only 78-79, AFH7879). That is WHY the LMC rep had nothing: it is not published anywhere for her to read. Do not treat her 'no information' as evasion, and do not expect a different rep to do better — RETRYING LMC REMAINS THE WRONG DOOR.

📐 2026-08-28 — **PAUL'S RULE: PRICE THE BOARD ALONE.** `paul-stated` — keep the math to the headliner only so vendors stay comparable; the dash kit and buckle sleeves are wants, not part of this decision, and bundling them made the comparison mushy. BOARD-ONLY DELIVERED:

⚠️ THE $50 IS STILL UNRESOLVED FROM LMC'S OWN SITE — the shipping FAQ (lmctruck.com/faq/shipping) loads its sections on demand and the text is not in the page, so it could not be read. The live cart still totals $546.88 with the oversize board in it and shows NO separate $50 line, but the cart is STEP 1 OF 5 (Cart → Shipping → Payment → Confirm → Complete) and oversize charges commonly appear at the SHIPPING step. RESOLVE IT at the checkout Shipping step or by asking LMC directly. Do not treat the cart total as final.

The key realization (2026-06-22): this is NOT a separate project — it's the first step of reassembly after paint, and nearly free in teardown terms because every surface it needs is already exposed by work you're already doing: door shells (panels off), floor pans (carpet up, seats out at the trim shop), roof (headliner down). Refinish sequence — Phase 4.

LAYER MODEL (researched 2026-07-27) — "sound deadening" is FOUR different jobs, and confusing them is how people waste money:
1. DAMPING — stop sheet metal ringing. Butyl/foil CLD (Kilmat, Noico, Resonix, Dynamat) straight onto bare metal. ~25–30% coverage on a large panel gets most of the benefit; full coverage is mostly wasted money and weight. Highest return per dollar on this truck.
2. DECOUPLING — thin closed-cell foam (CCF) over the CLD so the barrier floats instead of being mechanically bridged to the metal.
3. BARRIER — mass loaded vinyl (MLV), ~1 lb/ft². This is the layer that actually blocks airborne road/exhaust noise. MLV laid without CCF under it loses most of its effect — that's the mistake to avoid, and it's also why the ACC bonded "mass backing" underperforms (see the Carpet entry).
4. ABSORPTION — jute / hydrophobic melamine, kills in-cabin reflections. The carpet's heat-bonded jute already IS this layer.

TWO ROOFS, OPPOSITE TREATMENTS — she has a steel cab roof over the front seats and a REMOVABLE FIBERGLASS HARDTOP over the rear (which is why vendors sell "cab headliner" and "removable hard top headliner" as separate parts). Front/steel: classic CLD territory — steel rings, so ~25% on the spans between the ribs, then a light absorber. Rear/fiberglass: fiberglass doesn't ring like steel, so CLD's return drops sharply — absorber for rain impact matters more, and WEIGHT IS A HARD CONSTRAINT because that top gets lifted off by hand. No MLV up there.

FLOOR + TUNNEL is where the thick stack pays. The transmission tunnel is the loudest AND hottest surface on a 351W truck, so MLV there doubles as a heat barrier.

RULES:
• NEVER lay butyl over rust or bare metal — it traps moisture and rots the pan under a sealed layer. Repair and paint first (the sequence already does this).
• Don't seal over the floor drain plugs. Water that gets in has to get out — especially with a removable top.
• Wipe every surface with isopropyl and use a roller. Contamination kills butyl adhesion, and unrolled CLD is decorative.
• The stack adds ~0.4" of floor height (CLD ~2mm + CCF ~6mm + MLV ~2.4mm) — see the fitment trap in the Carpet entry before committing thickness anywhere.

SEQUENCE: rust repair → interior paint → CLD → CCF → MLV (floor/tunnel, not the top) → carpet + headliner in.

CORRECTION 2026-07-27 — an earlier pass here over-specified the prep. Butyl needs a CLEAN, SOUND surface, NOT a freshly painted one. Intact factory coating is actually the better substrate because it's already cured. So the prep is a FORK you take after looking, not a fixed ritual: just dirty → vacuum, degrease, dry, deaden, same session, no cure gate (the likely case); surface rust or flaking → treat it, but for the panel's survival, not the deadener's, because sealing rust under butyl is how you find a hole in five years; perforated → different job entirely. PAINT ONLY BUYS A CURE GATE, and in this build the gate is FREE — the panels and interior are apart for the shop anyway, so there are months, not a weekend. Painting hidden cavities because you want them clean is a perfectly good reason; it just isn't a requirement.

CAVITY WAX — after deadening, shoot Fluid Film / Woolwax into the bottoms of the doors (and any other closed cavity that's open) and confirm the drains run. Doors and rockers rot bottom-up from the INSIDE, and this teardown is the only time that access will ever exist. ~$20. Order matters: deaden first, wax after — you cannot deaden over wax.

PAINTED CARGO FLOOR CHANGES THE REAR PLAN — with the bed staying body-colour (see 'Carpet'), there's no hidden layer to stack on top back there, so rear-floor treatment moves to the UNDERSIDE of the bed floor, applied from beneath the truck. No MLV in the cargo area at all if the floor shows.

Door specifics live with the teardown protocol in guides/bolores-door-panel-repair.md (STEP 6): don't seal the door drains, and go easy on mass in a door — OBS Ford doors are heavy and sag-prone, so CLD on the outer skin + foam on the inner, not a pile of MLV.

CARGO FLOOR — REVISED 2026-07-27 (supersedes the painted-floor note directly above, which assumed an exposed bed, AND a since-removed note that assumed original paint was being preserved). ACTUAL STATE: the bed gets a FRESH factory-colour respray and then CARPET over it. So there is no original-paint constraint back there and no reason to avoid bonding — the cargo floor is treated like any other floor: CLD bonded on top, CCF, MLV, carpet. Simpler and acoustically better than the loose-laid workaround that was briefly recorded here.

THE REAL CONSTRAINT IS THE CURE GATE — that bed paint is FRESH, so butyl doesn't go on it until it has fully cured, or the solvent still outgassing underneath lifts the deadener later. Costs nothing here: the truck is apart anyway (see the free-cure-gate note above).

✅ CARGO FLOOR RESOLVED 2026-07-27 (Paul) — NOTHING GETS BONDED BACK THERE. The cargo carpet simply RESTS on the painted bed; no adhesive, no deadener bonded to the floor. This is also how molded kits normally go in — the cargo section is held by its own molded shape plus the wheel-well covers, sill plates and belt bolts; gluing is mostly a front-footwell/tunnel thing where carpet wants to creep.

Three things fall out, all favourable: (1) it makes the WATER story better, not just simpler — the standing 'pull the rear carpet after a real soaking' practice (see 'Carpet') is only possible with loose carpet; bonded carpet can't be lifted and dried, and this truck has the leak history that makes that matter; (2) the REVEAL survives — lift it, see the fresh Scarlet Red, which was the point of carpeting rather than leaving it bare; (3) NO CURE GATE back there, so the bed's respray timing stops constraining anything.

THE TRADE: no CLD damping on the cargo floor. It's a big flat panel and it will drum a little. Spend nothing on it now — it's the least important surface back there, the carpet's jute gives absorption, and the transmission tunnel is what actually gets noticed. The fix stays fully available later and never touches the paint: DAMP IT FROM THE UNDERSIDE, worked from beneath the truck. Revisit only when the amp + subs go in (Phase 5) — bass on an undamped floor is the one case where it'd be audible.

If the mat ever wanders under loading: hook-and-loop tabs or snap fasteners give retention without committing to adhesive.

⭐ HOW TO ACTUALLY CLEAN THE METAL — added 2026-08-09, and it SUPERSEDES the one-line 'wipe every surface with isopropyl' in the RULES above, which is the single most common way this job fails. IPA ALONE DOES NOT REMOVE OIL, SILICONE OR UNDERCOATING RESIDUE — it thins them and spreads them. Butyl then bonds to the contaminant instead of the steel, and the contaminant lets go. Do it in three stages:
1. MECHANICAL FIRST. Shop-vac, then scrape the old jute/tar factory pad with a PLASTIC scraper and a heat gun on LOW. Roloc bristle disc or wire wheel on any scale. ⚠️ A half-removed tar remnant is WORSE than an untouched panel — the deadener bonds to the remnant, and the remnant is what fails.
2. TWO-STAGE CHEMICAL WIPE. First WAX & GREASE REMOVER (SEM 38374, Eastwood PRE, or Klean-Strip Prep-All) to lift the oils; THEN an IPA flash wipe to remove the remover. ⭐ TWO-RAG RULE ON BOTH STAGES: solvent on rag #1, dry rag #2 wipes it off BEFORE IT EVAPORATES. Wiping it on and letting it dry re-deposits everything just dissolved. This one habit is most of the difference.
3. TEMPERATURE — the second-biggest failure mode and the one nobody plans for. Butyl adhesion is thermally gated: panel AND sheets both want to be ≥65°F. Warm the CLD in the sun or a heated room first. Cold metal plus a cold sheet gives a bond that looks perfect and releases in a Georgia August.
Then ROLL IT HARD until the foil dimples flatten. ▶️ VERIFY, don't assume: press a 2x2" offcut, wait 10 minutes, try to peel a corner. If it lifts clean, the surface is not clean — find out now and not from behind glued-down carpet.
⚠️ NEVER deaden over rust, over cracked seam sealer, or over a partially-removed factory pad.
📍 NOTE 2026-08-09: the interior sheet metal is now going BODY-COLOUR in Larry's scope (see 'Full repaint'). That largely RETIRES this procedure for the cab floor — fresh cured paint is the ideal substrate and needs only a degrease. Keep the procedure: it still governs every surface the shop does NOT spray, which is the door cavity interiors and the rocker insides.

✅ MATERIAL ON SHELF (found 2026-08-28, was in NO record): CUKWUYBY butyl CLD, 80 mil, 36 sq ft / 33 sheets (Amazon B0F1MV7GRF, bought 2026-02-23 — the day BEFORE the roller already on file, which is why the mat was missed). That is LAYER 1 (damping) fully stocked; it goes on METAL and is still gated on Larry (heat/filler on a door skin cooks butyl applied behind it). LAYER 2 (decoupling) is a DIFFERENT material — closed-cell foam, ordered 2026-08-28 — and butyl is not a substitute for it.

restoration.item: ⭐ Colour spray-out test — ONE bench test that gates the carpet order AND the interior spray
restoration.detail:
ADDED 2026-08-05 (Paul: roll the colour tests into the physical work — they are a bench task in the sequence, not a decision sitting in a queue). Cost is one aerosol can of SEM 4168, a scrap panel, and one hour of daylight. NO PARTS, NO SHOP, NO GATE ABOVE IT — this can be done on any clear afternoon, long before anything comes apart.

⭐ WHY IT IS ONE TEST AND NOT THREE: the record carried what LOOKED like a contradiction — the carpet row says match the AFTERMARKET LEATHER, 'NOT the 1989 factory chart', while the 2026-08-04 colour work says order the kit against FACTORY Chestnut, 'not against today's faded interior'. Both are correct because they govern DIFFERENT SURFACES, and reading them side by side is what makes them look like a conflict:
  • INTERIOR TRIM (dash, door panels, pillars, kick panels) → becomes SEM 4168, factory Chestnut. Documented and reproducible.
  • SEATS → aftermarket leather of unknown hide (reupholstered in the Edwards era; see 'Driver seat upholstery'). Not factory, and no chart predicts it.
  • CARPET → has to live between the two, and it is the only one of the three you cannot redo.

SO THE REFERENCE IS NOT 'the factory chart' AND NOT 'the interior as it looks today' — it is a SPRAYED-OUT CARD OF WHAT THE TRIM IS ABOUT TO BECOME. Today's panels are 37 years faded and are being sprayed over; judging a permanent carpet purchase against a surface that is about to stop existing is the specific mistake this step removes.

THE TEST: (1) spray one can of SEM 4168 on scrap — ideally a piece of the same plastic, primed as the shop will prime it — and let it fully cure, because Color Coat shifts as it dries; (2) order the free ACC swatches now (Bronco Graveyard / Stock Interiors — free, no commitment, and the long pole is shipping, so send for them today); (3) lay the cured 4168 card, the carpet swatches, and the actual leather seat together IN DAYLIGHT, not under shop light. Photograph the three together for the record.

ACCEPTANCE: a named carpet colour that Paul has seen against both the sprayed trim colour and the leather, in daylight. Not a code, not a vendor name on a screen.

⚠️ WHY THIS GATE EARNS ITS PLACE — ACC charges a 30% RESTOCKING FEE, so the carpet is a ONE-SHOT purchase (~$339–363, i.e. ~$100+ to be wrong). And it gates in the other direction too: the shop sprays the trim panels, so if the test says 4168 fights the leather, that is worth knowing BEFORE the panels are shot, not after. It is the cheapest step in the whole interior and it is upstream of the two most expensive irreversible ones.

GATES: 'Carpet — molded kit' (do not order until this passes) and the interior-trim half of 'Full repaint'. GATED BY: nothing. Independent of the tire-carrier swap and of all bodywork — it does not wait on the teardown sequence and should not be held behind it.

Researched + decided 2026-07-27. A MOLDED, VEHICLE-SPECIFIC KIT IS THE CALL — not bulk roll carpet. The realistic alternative means templating and seaming a two-door Bronco's tunnel and wheel wells by hand: days of work for a worse result, and the kit costs less than a trim shop's labor alone.

WHAT TO BUY — the vendors are reselling ONE product: Auto Custom Carpets (ACC), made in USA. Bronco Graveyard $339 (listed 87–93); Stock Interiors $362.95 (87–96, base plush cut pile). LMC sells the same class of kit and is very likely also ACC-sourced, but that's unconfirmed — their site blocks automated reads (403), so LMC's price is UNVERIFIED. So you're choosing a retailer and a spec, not a brand; Bronco Graveyard is cheapest of the three for the same kit.

WHAT THE "COMPLETE" KIT INCLUDES: passenger area + rear cargo + wheel well covers, with mildew-resistant jute heat-bonded to the back where padding was factory, and the heel pad positioned. NO padding in the rear cargo area.

DECIDED — SKIP THE MASS BACKING (+$125 Bronco Graveyard / +$145 Stock Interiors). It's a thin rubber layer bonded to the carpet, FRONT SECTION ONLY, and being glued to the carpet it can't be decoupled — a compromised version of the MLV layer the soundproofing build does properly and cheaper. Forum owners also report the mass-backed version is noticeably harder to make lie flat. (If the full CLD/CCF/MLV build ever gets abandoned, mass backing becomes the cheap shortcut — that's the only case for it.)

KNOWN FIT ISSUES (fullsizebronco.com): molding is "not very well defined like original" — it arrives oversized in places and you trim it down. The TRANSMISSION TUNNEL is the trouble spot (one owner with the bigger E4OD hump gave up and covered the tunnel separately; the AOD hump is smaller, so lower risk — but test-fit the tunnel before cutting anything). WHEEL-WELL COVERS are the fiddliest piece, a two-person job — check the overlap with the rear section before cutting. Cutting the holes (seat bolts, belt anchors, shifter, 4WD lever) is the hard part: measure from underneath, cut small, open up. Heat gun or steamer to re-mold the backing to the pan. It settles over a few days once the seats bolt down and hold it flat.

⚠️ FITMENT TRAP — the deadening stack raises the floor ~0.4", and the carpet was molded for FACTORY thickness. Put the thick stack where it pays (tunnel + flat floor), keep it thin in the footwells and away from the pedals, and keep it OUT FROM UNDER THE SEAT RISER FEET entirely — do NOT solve a raised floor with longer bolts, because seat and belt anchors are structural and thread engagement isn't the place to improvise. Test-fit the carpet over the FINISHED deadening before cutting a single hole.

COLOR GATE — ⛔ SUPERSEDED-IN-PLACE 2026-08-05: this gate is now the '⭐ Colour spray-out test' item immediately above, which resolves it rather than restating it. Read that row before ordering. The sentence below is preserved because it is HALF the answer and was never wrong — it governs the SEATS; the sprayed trim is the other half, and the test judges the carpet against BOTH at once. Original wording: match the AFTERMARKET LEATHER and the sprayed chestnut, NOT the 1989 factory chart (see 'Driver seat upholstery': the seats aren't factory). ACC charges a 30% RESTOCKING FEE on returned carpet, so there's one shot: order the free swatches now and judge them in daylight against the leather. (Forum datapoint, UNVERIFIED: '89 Eddie Bauer tan trim = "Light Chestnut," code 9T.)

SEQUENCE — Phase 4, and LAST: order swatches now, but buy only after the floor is painted and the deadening is in. Gate cleared 2026-07-27: the tailgate leak itself is fixed (see 'Bed rust'), so the remaining gate is the metal repair + paint.

⚠️ COLLISION SURFACED 2026-07-27 — THE BED IS STAYING CABERNET RED (see 'Full repaint'), and the ACC "complete kit" carpets the passenger area PLUS REAR CARGO PLUS WHEEL WELLS. You can't spray the bed body-colour to show it off and then carpet over it. DECIDE BEFORE ORDERING — it changes which kit gets bought:
• Carpeted cargo area — more original for an Eddie Bauer, quieter, warmer. Hides the red.
• Painted cargo area — sportier and more truck-like, easy to hose out, better for hauling.
• MIDDLE PATH (looks deliberate on a Bronco, and is the recommendation): carpet the WHEEL WELLS and side panels — which are the big resonant surfaces anyway — leave the FLOOR red, and throw a removable mat over it when hauling.

CONSEQUENCE — a visible painted floor has nowhere to hide the deadening stack. No CCF/MLV on top of a show surface, so rear treatment has to move to the UNDERSIDE of the bed floor, worked from beneath the truck. Different job, different product; plan it in rather than discovering it.

UNCONFIRMED, worth a phone call to Bronco Graveyard before ordering: whether a PASSENGER-AREA-ONLY kit even exists for this truck. Every vendor listing found is "complete kit" (ACC lists complete kits across 87-93 and 94-96; Stock Interiors' category page 404'd). Cargo-area pieces ARE sold separately elsewhere, so a front-only kit probably exists — but it isn't verified.

Also unverified: whether the kit includes a tailgate cover — some ACC listings explicitly exclude it.

✅ DECIDED 2026-07-27 (Paul) — BUY THE COMPLETE KIT, rear cargo carpeted. The bed is factory-COLOURED and is getting a fresh respray in that colour (see 'Full repaint' — an earlier reading here had it as preserved original paint; that was an agent misread, corrected same day). His call is to re-cover it: carpet goes back over the fresh paint, protecting it, and lifts out any time he wants to look at the bed. That also resolves the collision above and moots the open "does a passenger-area-only kit exist" question — complete is what every vendor sells anyway, so it's one less call. It restores the absorber layer for the audio build, and it's the Eddie Bauer-correct answer, which lines up with the factory-two-tone-protects-resale logic already driving the paint.

MAINTENANCE PRACTICE that comes with the decision: carpet + jute over the bed floor will hold water against the paint if water gets in, and this truck has exactly that history. Keep the bed drains clear, and treat "pull the rear carpet after a real soaking" as a standing practice — the removability is doing double duty, not just serving as a party trick.

📍 2026-07-27 (Paul): the OLD interior carpeting is ALREADY OUT — he stripped it, cargo floor is bare. So nothing is holding moisture against the floor any more, and the new kit lands on a clean slate whenever the floor work and paint are done.

The everyday listening system is in and playing — installed together ~Feb 2026. All four speakers run STRAIGHT OFF THE HEAD UNIT; the truck's old external amp didn't work and was pulled.

⭐ HEAD UNIT — ESTABLISHED FROM THE RECEIPT 2026-08-09: a RetroSound "Build A DIN Radio", variant MOTOR 2B / BLACK. Retro Manufacturing order #116059, placed 2026-01-20, delivered 2026-01-27, $384.19 total (radio $296.99 + Black Dot Knob Set $42.99 + shipping/protection/tax).

⚠️ THIS CARD SAID "RetroSound (Liberty-type)" FOR SIX MONTHS AND IT WAS WRONG. The Liberty was the front-runner in a Dec-2025 shopping thread — "pending decision" — and the intake filed it under "🔩 Part-number leads (UNVERIFIED — model inference)." The hedge word "-type" carried the uncertainty correctly; what failed is that nobody went and got the receipt for six months, and a hedged guess reads like a fact once it has sat in a card long enough. Same failure shape as "Cabernet Red." The receipt was in Gmail the whole time.

MOTOR 2B — the three specs everything else depends on (manual now held on disk, see below):
• Internal amp: 25 W RMS x4 / 45 W max x4 @14.4V @4Ω @1% THD.
• ⭐ MULTI-CHANNEL PRE-AMP OUTPUTS: FRONT, REAR **and SUBWOOFER**. The sub RCA is switchable (SUB ON/OFF), has its own level (SUB VOL 0-12) and a selectable crossover point of 80 / 120 / 160 Hz — all from the dash. This is what makes the amp/sub build straightforward.
• ⭐ SEPARATE power-antenna AND AMPLIFIER TURN-ON leads — a dedicated remote lead already exists.
• Rated output impedance 4Ω · low-level output 2.85V · 10.5-14.4V · max 15A · <3.5mA key-off · Radio Motor body 3.96"W x 1.98"H x 4.30"D, radio FACE only 3.5"W x 1.5"H · Bluetooth hands-free + streaming · rear USB (MP3/WMA/FLAC, 2.1A charge) · 30 presets + RDS · 32,000-colour display · non-volatile memory · 1-year warranty.

SPEAKERS — FRONT doors: Infinity Kappa 63XF 6.5" (165 mm) two-way coax, 85W RMS / 255W peak, 3Ω, 93 dB, 45 Hz-40 kHz, on NVX XBAF65 silicone baffles (open-box, Creative Audio order #1000140355, Feb 2026, $149.99). REAR: Infinity Kappa 86CFX 6x8 two-way coax, 100W RMS / 300W peak, 2.5Ω, 94 dB, 40 Hz-25 kHz (Creative Audio bundle). The front openings turned out to be 6.5" ROUND — diagnosed from photos mid-install after a 6x8 was assumed — which is why the truck runs two different sizes rather than a matched set.

⚠️⚠️ IMPEDANCE MISMATCH — LOGGED 2026-08-09, NOT A FAULT TODAY BUT THE REASON THE AMP MATTERS. The Motor 2B is rated for a 4Ω load. The fronts are 3Ω and the rears are 2.5Ω, so ALL FOUR CHANNELS ARE DRIVING BELOW SPEC, the rears substantially. RetroSound's own manual names this exact condition as a fault cause (FAQ p.19: "Speaker impedance below 4 ohms. Older speakers are usually not compatible with modern electronics."), and its troubleshooting table lists "internal amp in protection mode" as a cause of the unit lighting up with no sound (p.18). It plays fine today and Paul's own read is that it sounds good — this is not a prediction of failure. What it IS: the head unit is being asked for more current than it is specified to deliver, continuously. ⭐ THE CONSEQUENCE: the external amp stops being a loudness upgrade and becomes the thing that moves an out-of-spec load off the head unit. And IF THE RADIO EVER CUTS OUT when warm or loud, suspect this FIRST — before the wiring, before the unit.

⚠️ 6x8 PURCHASE — TWO BUNDLES, ONE UNRESOLVED. EXTRACTED.md records order #1000140240 (2/24, $228.68) AND a second 6x8 bundle inside #1000140355 (2/25, $219.99). The intake also carries an unclosed loop — "torn surround on one new speaker; thread doesn't confirm whether it was exchanged." A replacement would explain it. So either a return happened or THERE IS AN UNUSED PAIR OF 6x8 KAPPAS somewhere. Worth finding before buying anything else.

📖 MANUALS NOW HELD (ingested 2026-08-09, do not re-download): manuals/text/bronco-1989-audio-motor2b.txt (26 pp, official) · bronco-1989-audio-din-install.txt (12 pp) · bronco-1989-audio-speakers.txt (compiled specs — Infinity blocks automated fetches, so the vendor PDFs are queued as 📥 rows in .private/service-records/bronco-1989/REFERENCE.md).

Reaching it means pulling the door card — which is already happening for the panel repair and deadening. Audition it then; afterwards it's a full disassembly to change a setting.

✅ SPARE-PAIR LOOP CLOSED 2026-08-09 (Paul, ground truth): THE UNUSED PAIR IS IN HIS GARAGE. So both 6x8 bundles were kept — no return happened — and the second purchase was the replacement for the torn-surround speaker found during the Feb-2026 install. ⭐ HIS CALL: REPAIR THE TEAR rather than write the pair off — "it's a pretty damn good set of speakers," and it is: a spare pair of 100W-RMS Kappa 86CFX. restoration.item: ⭐ Head unit mounting — DIN sleeve (the radio is currently ZIP-TIED IN)
restoration.detail:
📍 GROUND TRUTH (Paul, 2026-08-09): the RetroSound is "just kind of zip tied in there." The faceplate question is CLOSED — Retro sent one free — but nothing mechanically holds the radio.

WHY IT DOESN'T HOLD, which is the part that was never understood: RetroSound's normal mounting is SHAFT NUTS + InfiniMount brackets + a metal BACKSTRAP — it hangs off two threaded shafts through holes in the dash face. A previous owner CUT THIS DASH to a 7x2" DIN opening for a Pioneer MVH-P8200BT, so there are no shaft holes for the shafts to pass through and the normal system has nothing to grab. Compounding it: the Motor 2B's radio FACE is only 3.5" x 1.5" while the opening is 7" x 2", so the face doesn't even cover the hole — which is exactly why a faceplate was needed as a separate part, and why the order arrived without one.

THE FIX — RetroSound UNIVERSAL DIN REPAIR KIT, $64.99. It supplies the DIN SLEEVE (cage) plus adapter brackets: the sleeve goes into the cut opening, the radio slides in until it clicks. That is the mounting path this truck needs, and it is the product Paul already identified.

✅ FITMENT — the two gates are cleared. (1) The kit lists Motor 1 / Motor 2 / Motor 4; this is a Motor 2B, in the Motor 2 family. (2) The kit requires a true DIN opening and a flat dash — PAUL'S GROUND TRUTH SETTLES IT: "the previous install had a DIN radio, so I know it will fit." 📍 GROUND TRUTH (Paul, 2026-08-09): THE SPARE PAIR IS IN THE GARAGE. This closes the open loop from the Feb-2026 install ('torn surround on one new speaker; thread doesn't confirm whether it was exchanged') and explains the two 6x8 bundle purchases — no return happened, the second bundle was the replacement. So the truck has a FULL SPARE PAIR of Infinity Kappa 86CFX (100W RMS, 2.5Ω, 94 dB), one of which has a small tear.

PAUL'S CALL: repair the tear rather than write the pair off — "it's a pretty damn good set of speakers." Agreed; a small surround tear is a genuinely repairable, ~$10, one-evening job, and the acoustic penalty of a competent repair is negligible.

▶️ FIRST, TELL SURROUND FROM CONE — it decides whether this is worth doing. A tear in the SURROUND (the flexible rubber roll at the outer edge) is routine. A tear in the CONE itself, or anything at the SPIDER or voice coil, is a different and much less rewarding job.

METHOD (surround tear):
1. Clean both faces of the tear with isopropyl on a cotton swab. Let it flash off fully.
2. Use a FLEXIBLE adhesive — speaker-surround adhesive (Parts Express and similar sell it by that name) or a vinyl/fabric/plastic flexible adhesive. ⛔ NOT cyanoacrylate/superglue: it cures RIGID and the repair simply re-tears at its own edge on the first hard excursion. ⛔ Not RTV silicone.
3. A clean tear: butt the edges and run a THIN bead on the BACK side. A ragged or larger tear: back it with a small patch cut from a COFFEE FILTER — the classic trick, because it conforms and adds almost no mass — bonded with the same adhesive.
4. ⭐ KEEP IT THIN AND KEEP IT SYMMETRIC. Added mass lowers Fs; mass added to ONE SIDE makes the cone rock rather than piston, which is audible as distortion. A glob is worse than the tear.
5. Cure a full 24 h before playing. Then bench-test at low volume before it goes anywhere.

WHAT THE PAIR IS FOR — worth deciding before the work, because it changes nothing about the repair but a lot about urgency: (a) shelf spares against a future failure (the honest default — the installed rears are the same model); (b) if the amp build ever goes 3-way or adds rear-cargo speakers, they are already on hand; (c) sell them. No decision needed now; the repair is cheap enough to do regardless and a repaired pair is worth more than a torn one in every branch.

The audio upgrade beyond head-unit-only, deliberately last (Phase 5) — after the door panels are solid and the deadening is done so it sings. Amp + sub NOT yet purchased (confirmed 2026-07-14).

✅ THE HEAD UNIT SUPPORTS THIS PROPERLY — resolved 2026-08-09 from the Motor 2B manual. It has FRONT, REAR **and SUBWOOFER** pre-amp outputs (2.85V), a switchable sub RCA with its own level (SUB VOL 0-12) and a dash-selectable 80/120/160 Hz crossover, PLUS a separate amplifier turn-on lead. No line-output converter, no signal splitting, sub level adjustable from the seat. Every path below is clean.

⭐ THE REAL ARGUMENT IS IMPEDANCE, NOT LOUDNESS. See the audio item above: the speakers are 3Ω front / 2.5Ω rear against a head unit rated for 4Ω. An outboard amp rated for 2Ω operation would be running INSIDE spec where the Motor 2B is not. ⛔ SO THE GATE ON ANY AMP PURCHASE IS 2-OHM STABILITY — a 4Ω-only amp just reproduces the same problem with a bigger power supply.

PATH A — RetroSound SUB8100 bundle, $399.99 (SUB-8100 8" powered sub w/ 100W built-in + a 4-channel 45W x4 Class D). One vendor, one manual, period-correct, made to fit under a vintage seat. ⚠️ BUT THE 4-CHANNEL HALF IS A BAD BUY HERE: 25W→45W is +2.6 dB, and doubling power is barely 'slightly louder' (≈10x is 'twice as loud'). At 93-94 dB sensitivity these speakers are already loud off the head unit. That's ~$200 for a change Paul would struggle to hear. RetroSound does not publish the Quadraphonic's impedance rating — ask before considering it.

PATH B ⭐ RECOMMENDED — POWERED SUB ONLY. One RCA from the Motor 2B's sub output to a powered sub. Highest audible improvement per dollar, per wire and per hour. What the truck lacks is bass, not midrange power — Paul's own read is the speakers 'sound good as-is.' Does NOT fix the impedance issue (the four speakers stay on the head unit), so it is the comfort answer, not the engineering answer.

PATH C — COMPACT 5-CHANNEL, ~$450-700 (Alpine / JL / Rockford class): ~75-100W x4 to the Kappas plus a 300-500W sub channel, one chassis, one power run. +5 to +6 dB on the mains, which IS audible — and it is the ONLY path that also takes the out-of-spec load off the head unit. If the impedance argument is given its real weight, this is the correct answer.

⭐ WIRING MAY ALREADY BE IN THE TRUCK. The previous Pioneer install left a green remote-turn-on wire and a red/white RCA run feeding the dead amp. So the standing 'PRE-RUN the amp/sub wiring during the Phase-2 door + interior teardown' move may be a RE-USE job, not a new pull. ⚠️ CAVEAT from the intake: amp ground location, speaker routing and inline-fuse presence were NEVER TRACED — verify before trusting any of it. Retro recommends 16-gauge speaker wire.

⭐ SUB PLACEMENT COUPLES TO THE DEADENING DECISION — the non-obvious one. Paul decided 2026-07-27 that NOTHING gets bonded to the cargo floor, and the Soundproofing item explicitly flags 'revisit only when the amp + subs go in — bass on an undamped floor is the one case where it'd be audible.' A sub in the CARGO AREA triggers that revisit (damping the bed floor from UNDERNEATH the truck — different job, different product). A sub UNDER THE FRONT SEAT largely does not. That is a real argument for under-seat that has nothing to do with sound quality. ⚠️ But under-seat competes with the Carpet item's fitment trap: the deadening stack raises the floor ~0.4" and NOTHING goes under the seat riser feet. Measure before committing to a box height.

⭐ PATH B HAS A CONCRETE PART, AND IT IS HALF THE BUNDLE PRICE (found 2026-08-09 in the LMC FD.88 catalogue already in the corpus). Part 38-8527-F, POWERED SUBWOOFER-8", 100 WATT, $199.99 — versus $399.99 for the RetroSound SUB8100 bundle, whose extra $200 buys the 4-channel amp the analysis above argues against. Very likely the same unit as the SUB-8100. Published spec: 8" driver in a rigid die-cast aluminium chassis (heat dissipation), built-in 100W amp / 200W max, frequency response 35-100 Hz, THD 0.08%, fully adjustable crossover 50-100 Hz, independent gain, 0/180-degree PHASE control, low-level RCA input OR high-level input via supplied harness, includes mounting brackets, wiring harness and a WIRED REMOTE BASS CONTROL. 1-year warranty.
⭐⭐ THE DIMENSION THAT DECIDES PLACEMENT: 9" x 2.75" x 13.75", 9 lbs. At 2.75" TALL this is a genuine under-seat candidate — which is the placement the deadening argument above already favours. NOTE: the Motor 2B's dash SUB VOL control makes the wired remote bass knob redundant — one fewer thing to find a home for in a 1989 interior. ⚠️ LMC prices expired 2026-08-03; part number good.

═══ ⭐ RECOMMENDATION — 2026-08-09 (agent-proposed, NOT yet Paul-ratified) ═══
Paul clarified the RetroSound links were EXAMPLES, not a constraint, so this is the open-market answer: JL AUDIO XDM700/5 + a compact SEALED PASSIVE 8", mounted UNDER THE SEAT.

⛔ THE HARD GATE THAT DOES MOST OF THE CHOOSING: 2-OHM STABILITY ON ALL FOUR MAIN CHANNELS — not just the sub channel, which is what most spec sheets advertise. The speakers are 3Ω front and 2.5Ω rear. A 4Ω-only amp reproduces the existing out-of-spec condition with a bigger power supply behind it, which is worse than doing nothing.

THE SHORTLIST (verified specs, 2026-08-09):
• ⭐ JL Audio XDM700/5 — 75W x4 @4Ω / 100W x4 @2Ω; sub 180W @4Ω / 300W @2Ω (min 1.5Ω sub). 2.05"H x 10.23"W x 7.09"D, 6.15 lb.
• Alpine PDX-V9 — 100W x4 + 500W x1, rated 2-4Ω. 2.5"H x 10.19"W x 8.375"D. More sub power, slightly larger, not marine. A legitimate alternative.
  ⚠️ CORRECTION LOGGED: an earlier pass suspected the PDX mains were 4Ω-ONLY. THEY ARE NOT — Alpine rates them 2-4Ω. The suspicion was wrong and would have wrongly eliminated a good amp.
• RetroSound Quadraphonic (in the $399.99 SUB8100 bundle) — 45W x4. RULED OUT: +2.6 dB over the head unit, and RetroSound does not publish its impedance rating.

WHY THE JL: (1) into THESE loads it makes ~100W x4, which lands almost exactly on the Kappas' 85W/100W RMS ratings — a matched system, not an over- or under-powered one; (2) it moves the out-of-spec load off the Motor 2B, which is the actual reason to do this at all; (3) at 2.05" it is the slimmest credible option, and under-seat height is the binding constraint.
⚠️ THE MARINE CLAIM IS NOT VERIFIED. XDM is JL's marine line and the removable hardtop + this truck's leak history make corrosion resistance a real consideration rather than paranoia — BUT the XDM700/5 spec sheet pulled 2026-08-09 does NOT state conformal coating. CONFIRM WITH JL before paying a marine premium. If it isn't meaningfully different, buy the XD700/5v2 (identical power and dimensions) and mount it somewhere dry.

THE SUB: a PASSIVE sub in a compact sealed box, NOT a powered sub. Pairing a 5-channel with a powered sub pays for amplification twice and leaves the 5th channel idle. Shallow-mount 8" under-seat; 10" only if seat clearance surprises you. ⚠️ MEASURE CLEARANCE AFTER THE DEADENING GOES DOWN, not before — the stack raises the floor ~0.4" and nothing goes under the seat riser feet (see 'Carpet'). Start the Motor 2B's sub crossover at 80 Hz (its lowest of 80/120/160) and do finer shaping with the amp's own low-pass.

⛔ TWO INSTALL CAUTIONS — the first is a safety item:
• REUSE THE SIGNAL, RUN NEW POWER. The old Pioneer install left a green remote-turn-on wire and an RCA run — reuse those, that is the free win. DO NOT REUSE THE POWER WIRE: its gauge, ground point and fusing were NEVER TRACED (the intake says so explicitly), and feeding a 700W amp through unknown wire is a fire risk, not a shortcut. New 4-gauge OFC, fused at the battery.
• SET GAINS LOW. The Motor 2B's pre-out is a strong 2.85V. Set gains with the head unit at ~3/4 volume; cranked gains are exactly what produces the alternator whine RetroSound's own FAQ describes (manual p.20), and the fix list there starts with 'gain controls turned all the way up.'

BUDGET: amp ~$700-800 · sub + enclosure ~$200-350 · wiring kit ~$100 → roughly $1,000-1,250.
THE HONEST CHEAPER ANSWER, if this is more than the truck deserves right now: the $199.99 8" powered sub (LMC 38-8527-F) straight off the sub pre-out. Most of the audible gain for a fifth of the money. It just leaves all four speakers on the out-of-spec head unit — a comfort fix rather than an engineering one, and that is a legitimate choice to make deliberately.

▶️ EITHER WAY, THE ONE MOVE THAT SAVES A SECOND TEARDOWN: pre-run the wiring during the PHASE-2 door + interior teardown, even though the gear goes in at Phase 5.

The plastic screw bosses that hold the rear-window up/down and rear-defrost switches into the trim (lower-left of the steering column) had cracked through over time, leaving the switches loose. Rebuilt the bosses using heat-shrink tubing as a sleeve/form and JB Weld to recreate threadable mounting posts. Switches now mount solidly — arguably more durable than the original brittle plastic. See technique: "Screw-boss rebuild."

0_DECISION_factory_over_scan.agentAssessment: CORRECT, and the earlier spectro recommendation was mis-scoped — a scan exists to make ONE NEW part match EXISTING parts, and an all-panels respray dissolves that constraint. Carried over without re-checking its premise.
0_DECISION_factory_over_scan.strongestArgument_notOriginallyStated: ⭐ A FACTORY COLOUR IS REPRODUCIBLE; A SCAN IS A SNAPSHOT. In ten years 'SEM 4168' still buys the same colour and a damaged panel is a cheap fix. A custom scanned mix only survives as long as someone keeps the formula card. For a truck Paul intends to keep, that asymmetry is the real argument.
0_DECISION_factory_over_scan.⚠️_THE_GAP: 'Repaint everything' is not quite true, and the exceptions dominate the view. SPRAYED: dash, door panels, pillars, kick panels, consoles. NOT SPRAYED: the SEATS (aftermarket leather), the CARPET (new ACC kit), headliner, belts, steering wheel. So the trim is not matching nothing — it is matching the seats and carpet, the two things not being painted. Failure mode: fresh factory Chestnut against 37-year-old leather that aged its own direction, making the seats read wrong.
0_DECISION_factory_over_scan.⭐_CONSEQUENCE: THE CARPET ORDER AND THE TRIM COLOUR ARE ONE DECISION, and they currently live in two different restoration items. If the ACC kit is ordered to match the interior as it looks TODAY while the trim is sprayed factory-fresh, the interior is split against itself. Choose both against factory Chestnut, together.
0_DECISION_factory_over_scan.deRisk: (1) Buy ONE can of SEM 4168 (~$20), spray a scrap or a hidden panel back, and hold it against the actual seats and a carpet sample in daylight — SEM formulates for 'good overall match viewed from a few feet away', which is fine when everything is the same paint but guarantees nothing against the leather. (2) Order the carpet SAMPLE before the kit and judge all three together.
