serviceHistory.summary: PASSENGER door trim panel OFF and on the bench; door shell opened. Findings: (1) the back-side insulation is RECYCLED COTTON SHODDY (colored flecks) covering the unsupported flat field — an anti-drum/anti-buzz layer, torn and partly detached. Removed. Replacement is 1/8" closed-cell foam cut from it as a template, NOT a new fiber pad and NOT butyl (different layer). (2) A metal washer a prior repair had SUPERGLUED around a torn screw hole was removed by twisting it in-plane — CA shears far better than it peels; the washer came off clean with NO plastic attached, and the cured CA ring left behind was scraped off. (3) Retainer clips still seated in their pockets — materially better than the driver panel — but the panel does have damage and small cracks (Paul-confirmed), so back-side reinforcement is in scope. (4) ⚠️ NO WATER SHIELD / vapor barrier on the door at all (Paul-confirmed from the panel-off photos): access holes open straight into the cabin, so one must be FABRICATED, not resealed, and the drains checked clear in the same session. Parts ordered same day: black butyl seal tape, 1/8" sponge neoprene CCF x2, panel clips x2. Method + full checklist: guides/bolores-door-panel-repair.md STEP 7.

Coolant drain, double flush & refill — DIY, in the driveway. ODOMETER 11,032.5 Paul-read the same day (see the odometer note — this is a reading on the post-2023 reset counter, not lifetime miles). Radiator drained at the petcock, then TWO full water-flush cycles: refill, run to operating temperature with the heater on max so the block AND the heater core circulate, shut down, cool, drain again. ⭐ THE DRAIN CAME OUT CLEAN — diluted green, no rust, no grit, no milkiness, no oil film. That is a meaningful three-way NEGATIVE on a truck whose 1989–2010 history is undocumented: no significant internal corrosion, no coolant-into-oil path (head or intake gasket), and no transmission-cooler seep inside the radiator core — the last one worth stating explicitly because the C6 runs its cooler through the radiator, so a cross-leak was a live possibility going in. Block drain plugs were DELIBERATELY NOT PULLED: on a 37-year-old iron block a seized pipe plug that snaps off is a far worse day than the ~2 qt per side it recovers, and two dilution cycles reach substantially the same place. Overflow bottle emptied and rinsed separately (it is a dead leg the petcock never reaches). Refill spec: FRAM GREEN low-silicate IAT concentrate (F1015, 1 U.S. gal jugs ×2, bought over the counter) cut to 50/50 with DISTILLED water — correct era chemistry for a 1989 Ford (conventional green, ESE-M97B44-A lineage); explicitly NOT an orange/Dex-Cool or a 'universal'. Concentrate goes in first and neat, because the several quarts of flush water the petcock cannot drain out of the block are already part of the final mix. ⏳ OPEN AT TIME OF WRITING — the refill was still in progress when this row was created. To close out: confirm the final mix on a hydrometer/refractometer (target −34°F or colder), confirm the burp completed (upper hose hot and firm, vents hot, level stable with cap off), and confirm the cold-level top-off the following morning. Until those three are confirmed the MIX is a plan, not a measurement — the drain findings above are the verified part of this row.

⏸ PAUSED MID-REFILL, evening of 2026-08-19 — STOPPED DELIBERATELY, NOT ABANDONED. State of the truck as she sits: ~7 quarts of FRAM green concentrate are IN the radiator, poured NEAT (jug 1 entire = 4 qt, then ~3/4 of jug 2 = ~3 qt). She is roughly 2 QUARTS SHORT of full. ~1 quart of concentrate is HELD IN RESERVE in jug 2 on purpose, so the mix can be corrected in either direction once it can actually be measured. 🚫 ENGINE NOT STARTED since the refill began, and NOT DRIVEN. Radiator cap sitting on loose (dirt/rain only, not sealed). Do not run her until the top-off and burp are done: trapped air lets the gauge read normal while a pocket sits against the thermostat. WHY PAUSED: no distilled water on hand, and finishing with TAP was declined — hard water puts minerals straight into a system that had just been flushed clean, which is the one shortcut in this job that undoes the afternoon's work. Boiling tap does NOT substitute (it concentrates minerals rather than removing them); dehumidifier/AC condensate and rainwater were also ruled out as engine-grade. TO FINISH (≈40 min): buy PRE-MIXED 50/50 GREEN conventional coolant — 1 gal, and top off with it directly, which removes the need for distilled water entirely and leaves the right product on the shelf for future top-offs. (Distilled water, or deionized from a parts counter, works equally well.) Then: top to the bottom of the filler neck → cap OFF, run with heater on MAX, burp until the level HOLDS STEADY at full operating temperature → hydrometer/refractometer, target −34°F or colder → correct with the reserve quart (weak) or more 50/50 (strong) → cap on, overflow bottle to the COLD line only → walk the petcock, both radiator hose clamps and the heater hose connections for leaks → re-check COLD the next morning and top off. EXPECTED LANDING ≈52–54% glycol, which is fine and slightly on the good side of 50/50 for an iron block. VOLUME CROSS-CHECK for tomorrow: total liquid back in should be ≈9 qt. Much less ⇒ air still trapped, keep burping. Much more ⇒ it is going somewhere, find the leak before driving.

✅ CLOSED 2026-08-21 (refill completed) and ROAD-VERIFIED 2026-08-24. Topped off with DISTILLED water, not the pre-mixed 50/50 that the pause note recommended — pre-mix was the convenience answer sized to having no distilled on hand, but on this fill distilled was the better chemistry: the neat concentrate already in the radiator had made the system glycol-heavy by design, and pre-mix would have added yet more glycol on top of it. ~0.5–0.67 U.S. gal ≈ 2–2.7 qt of distilled went in. BURP CONFIRMED on all three independent signals — upper radiator hose hot, level STABLE at full operating temperature with the cap off, and the heater vents blowing genuinely hot. That third signal is the one that matters most and is the one usually skipped: the heater core is a dead leg the petcock never reaches, and hot air is the only proof it actually filled. ⭐ VOLUME CROSS-CHECK PASSED: ~7 qt concentrate + ~2.3 qt distilled ≈ 9.3 qt total back in, against the ≈9 qt predicted before the refill started. That one number clears BOTH failure modes the cross-check exists to catch — she did not swallow significantly more than predicted (no leak) and did not come up short (no trapped air pocket).

⚠️ THE MIX REMAINS INFERRED, NOT MEASURED. No hydrometer or refractometer was ever bought, so the −34°F target was never read on an instrument. Volume arithmetic: ~7 qt neat concentrate, plus only ~0.25 qt of glycol riding in the ~8% old-coolant residual that survived TWO flush cycles, over a ~15.5–16 qt system ⇒ ≈45–48% glycol, ≈ −29°F to −33°F. That is a safe and serviceable band — corrosion protection holds above ~40% and north Georgia's record low is near −17°F — but it lands a hair LEANER than the −34°F target. (It is also leaner than a first estimate made on 2026-08-24 of ~50%, which wrongly assumed a single flush cycle; the record's 'two cycles' is correct and the transcript confirms three total drains.) If a hydrometer later reads weak, the ~1 qt of FRAM concentrate deliberately held in reserve is the correction, and this row should be re-stamped then. Until an instrument reads it, the percentage is arithmetic and must not be promoted to a verified figure.

🛣 ROAD TEST 2026-08-24 — Jasper → Atlanta, ~60 miles including sustained mountain grade. Temperature gauge NEVER EXCEEDED THE 1/3 MARK. Paul's account of prior behaviour: a stable 1/2, climbing further on the grades. ⭐ THIS RESOLVED THE PRESENTING COMPLAINT — the running-warm symptom is what sent Paul into the cooling system on 8/19 in the first place, and it had never been written down anywhere in this record. See maintenance.coolingBaseline. Running COOLER under load is also weak independent corroboration that the mix did not land glycol-heavy: above ~50/50 heat transfer gets WORSE, so a 60%-glycol outcome would have shown equal or higher temperatures, not lower.

items.item: Repeated no-start — root cause NOT established
items.status: open — investigating. Presentation is consistently slow/labored crank, then nothing or a single click. Charging the battery has restored starting EVERY time so far, which points at charge state; the honest counterexample is 2025-05-09, when the battery was fully charged and the cause was still fuel. ⭐ NARROWED 2026-08-30 (observation, still not a diagnosis): three starts in ~1 hour, each shut off quickly — the engine FIRED ALL THREE TIMES while cranking power decayed monotonically to barely-turning. Fuel, spark and carb are exonerated FOR THIS EPISODE; it is on the electrical axis. ⚠️ Partly self-inflicted — a short idle run on this bike is a net WITHDRAWAL (headlight always on, 150 W only at 5 000 r/min), so three of them is a discharge test. Also 8/30: she was left with a trickle charger ATTACHED BUT UNPOWERED and lost charge — a charger with no blocking diode back-feeds through its own output stage. Neither observation is a verdict; both are now testable. ⭐ 2026-09-01, FLEET LAP 2 — THE PATTERN IN THIS VERY FIELD IS NOW FALSIFIED. Paul, verbal: "after charging the 200 for a good amount and then left it overnight and tried to start it and it would not start… the battery kind of dimmed and it sounded like I was trying to turn over… it just wound up clicking." So "charging has restored starting EVERY time so far" NO LONGER HOLDS: a full charge did not survive one night. That is a DIFFERENT CLAIM from charge STATE — it says the battery is not HOLDING, or something drained it. It is an UNINSTRUMENTED T4 (overnight-hold) failure; ⚠️ the clean T4 for that night is GONE, because it was cranked repeatedly before any reading was taken. ⚠️ Paul's read of the confound is HEDGED — "I don't think the bike was plugged into the charger" — so the 2026-08-30 back-feed hypothesis is WEAKENED, NOT EXCLUDED; T5's A/B settles it by measurement. ✅ The charger IS now identified: NEXPEAK NC201 PRO, a 7-stage smart charger with AGM/GEL and pulse-repair modes — NOT the dumb trickle that hypothesis assumed [photo-MODEL-READ 2026-09-01, unverified]. Protocol, thresholds and results log: guides/blue-thunder-starting-diagnosis.md. ⭐⭐ 2026-09-05, FLEET LAP 3 — THE AMBIGUITY THIS FIELD HAS CARRIED SINCE 8/30 IS BROKEN, BY MEASUREMENT. T4 RAN and PASSED: rested 12.64 V at 09-04 21:07:13 → 12.55 V at 09-05 09:46:19, a drop of 0.09 V over 12 h 39 m, inside T4's ±0.1 V band (EXIF-timestamped photographs; the two voltages are photo reads, the DELTA is the finding). So the battery HOLDS ITS CHARGE OVERNIGHT and there is NO PARASITIC DRAIN — T5 is retired unless something resurfaces it. Thirteen seconds after the 12.55 she collapsed to 9.41 V on a start attempt and clicked (paul-stated, his figure). ⭐ HOLDS VOLTAGE, CANNOT DELIVER CURRENT — those two together are high internal resistance, and they also RESOLVE the 09-01 falsification recorded above: 'a full charge did not survive one night' was inferred from a failed start with no meter. Today's measured hold says it held then too. ONE mechanism, not two. ⚠️ 9.41 is below T2's 9.5 V floor but she was at ~78%, not full — NOT promoted to a verdict; what changed is that a partial charge can flatter a good reading and cannot flatter a bad one, so 9.41 is a FLOOR on the capacity. 👤 OPEN, not guessed: was it read with the starter button HELD or AFTER release? Under load it is a textbook T2 reading; still 9.41 after release is far worse. ✅ paul-decided 2026-09-05: REPLACE THE BATTERY. Full audit in the guide.
items.whyItMatters: The labored-crank-then-click sequence is what a 6 Ah battery does under repeated cranking REGARDLESS of why the engine failed to fire, so it cannot distinguish 'she walked up to a low battery' from 'she cranked a healthy battery flat trying to start it for a fuel reason'. By the third attempt the evidence is gone either way. Mom is also riding on an unknown fuel level — this bike has no fuel gauge and reserve is only 2.5 L (0.7 gal).
items.check: Two observations, both taken BEFORE the battery is run down: (1) resting voltage before the first crank of the day — >=12.4 V means it was not the battery; (2) ⚠️ CORRECTED 2026-08-30 — there is NO KICKSTARTER (paul-verified; the manual claiming one is a DR200SE manual). The substitute is the AVAPOW jump pack in the kit: clip it on at the FIRST labored crank — fires on the pack = engine/fuel/spark are fine and it was purely charge. Standing rule for Mom: three attempts of five seconds, then stop. ⭐ 8/30 — the discriminator is now T2, CRANKING VOLTAGE ON A FULLY CHARGED BATTERY: a dying AGM reads 12.6 V happily (surface charge is free) but collapses below ~9.5 V under the starter. That single 30-second test separates 'battery has no capacity left' from 'it was spent faster than it could be replaced'.

restoration.item: Fall put-away — oil change + drain the carb
restoration.detail: Autumn 2026, a fall evening in the shop. Paul's call 2026-07-27, and it's the better order: fresh oil sits far better over winter than used oil, which carries a little acid and moisture the whole time it sits. So this REPLACES the spring oil change rather than adding to it. Calendar reminder set for the first Saturday of November, recurring yearly — but the date is a placeholder for "too cold to ride," not a deadline; move it to whichever evening the riding actually ends (first frost here averages Oct 17). THE JOB: warm her up, drain the oil, new filter (Suzuki 16510-37450 / HiFlo HF138), refill ~1.0 qt 10W-40 JASO MA/MA2. Then DRAIN THE FLOAT BOWL on the Mikuni BST31SS — this is the one that actually matters for her. Stale fuel varnishing in the carb is exactly what cost her the drain-and-flush in May 2025, and an empty bowl can't varnish. Tires to 22 psi front / 25 rear, chain cleaned and lubed. BOTH BIKES: fill the tank most of the way with the ethanol-free gas they already run — less air space, less condensation. Battery off the bike, on a tender or somewhere it won't freeze (that's what worked last time). Cover her. ⭐ NEW 2026-08-30 — CARBURETOR REFURBISH RIDES ALONG WITH THIS EVENING: see the separate restoration item below. Draining the bowl is no longer the whole carb job; if the kit is on the shelf, rebuild rather than just drain.

Spring 2027. If the fall put-away went as above, this is a small morning, not a project: battery back on, fresh fuel, prime the carb, check tires and chain, ride. A full carb clean should NOT be needed — draining the bowl in the fall is what buys that. Only pull the bowl if she runs lean or won't idle, which points at a clogged pilot circuit. Float height spec, if you ever are in there: 13.0 ± 1.0 mm.

Replaced with new 7/8" (22 mm) handlebars. Closes the bent-bar item — per the prior call, a re-bent steel bar is permanently weakened, so replace beats re-straighten. New levers fitted at the same time.

restoration.item: Carburetor refurbish — Mikuni BST31SS rebuild kit
restoration.detail: Paul's call 2026-08-30, prompted by the fuel seepage we keep seeing. DO IT AT THE NEXT DECOMMISSION — it rides along with the fall put-away, since she is already down and the bowl is already coming off. They make rebuild kits for this carb. WHAT A KIT BUYS: float needle and seat, bowl gasket and o-rings, and usually jets — i.e. it closes the float-needle branch outright, which matters twice over: it is the part that would let her flood overnight with the petcock left on (the flooding hypothesis in the starting investigation), and it is the part the leaning-weep technique names as its own falsifier. ⚠️ ORDER BY THE I.D. NUMBER STAMPED ON THE CARB BODY, NOT THE MODEL NAME: the manual lists TWO ids for the same BST31SS — 42AC (E-03/E-28) and 42AE (E-33/California). Read the stamp first. MANUAL-VERIFIED SPECS to check the kit and the rebuild against: bore 31 mm; float height 13.0 ± 1.0 mm; idle 1 500 ± 100 r/min; pilot screw PRE-SET from the factory (expect a limiter cap — plan for removing it if the kit expects the screw to be re-set). ⚠️ JET SIZES ARE NOT SAFE TO ORDER FROM OUR ON-DISK COPY: in manuals/text/dr200s-2017-service.txt the carburetor table's columns are scrambled by the text extraction — the values #125 / 5D77 / #25 do not align cleanly to the M.J. / J.N. / P.J. rows. Read the real table before ordering jets. ⛔ THIS DOES NOT OVERTURN the leaning-weep technique, which stays 'normal for a carbureted bike on a hard-leaning sidestand'. The refurb is preventive maintenance taken at the cheapest moment, not a diagnosis of a bad seal. What WOULD be a diagnosis: weeping on level ground or at only a mild lean.

techniques.name: She weeps fuel when parked at a steep lean — park her level
techniques.method: Wheels sitting higher than the kickstand, or nose-down on a slope, tips the float bowl past the level of its vent and she'll seep a little fuel from the carburetor overflow, right beside the bowl drain screw. Roll her onto flat ground and it stops. Normal for a carbureted bike on a hard-leaning sidestand — not a bad seal, and no part to buy. Habit worth keeping: fuel valve off when she's parked on anything sloped, and don't fill the tank right up into the filler neck if she's going to sit in the sun. WHAT WOULD CHANGE THE STORY: if she ever weeps on level ground, or starts spilling at only a mild lean, the bowl level is riding high — check float height (spec 13.0 ± 1.0 mm) and the float needle seat.

restoration.item: Electrical fault — total power loss when steering
restoration.detail:
RESOLVED 2026-07-03 — Paul got the power-loss fault worked out; the bike powers up cleanly again with a constant, steady flow. THE ACTUAL FIX (not the planned conductor splice): worked the connectors up by the steering head — reseated the individual wires/pins in their plastic connector housings, cleaned the contacts with electrical contact cleaner, then pressed the connectors firmly back together; that alone restored a constant flow. Also patched a couple of questionable wire joints and wrapped everything in electrical tape for a more durable seal. So the root cause was really dirty/loose connector contacts at the flex point, not a cleanly-broken conductor. WATCH FOR RECURRENCE: the tape seal is less permanent than adhesive-lined heat-shrink, and if the fault ever returns when turning the bars, the fallback is to cut the suspect section back to bright copper and solder-splice it with adhesive heat-shrink (the originally-planned repair).

— Original diagnosis, kept for reference —
DIAGNOSED 2026-06-13 — traced end to end with a multimeter. The fault is a broken/fatigued conductor in the steering-head harness (the bundle that flexes when you turn the bars), confirmed by wiggle-testing the wires and watching the headlight cut on and off. THE TRAIL: (1) Battery good — 12.7V at the posts, both cables tight. (2) Main fuse good — there are two 20A blade fuses in the holder above the battery; the live one reads 12.7V on BOTH ends (power passes all the way through it), the second is just Suzuki's spare clipped in an unwired holder (reads nothing — normal). So power is healthy from the battery through the fuse. (3) Followed the feed forward to the green 2-pin connector up by the bars (a red wire + an orange wire): the RED wire is the always-hot feed and reads 12.7V there — power is good right up to the steering head. (4) Wiggling the harness at the steering head makes the headlight flicker on and off = a make-and-break in a conductor right where the bundle flexes with steering. This matches the original 'died when I turned the bars' symptom, and the water that killed the speedo points to the same area. ORIGINAL SYMPTOM (first test ride, June 2026): leaned the bike, turned the bars, and ALL power died at once — headlight cut instantly, no response to ignition on/off. The speedo was already removed + taped off during that ride, so a speedo short was ruled out. The carbureted DR-Z400S has no tip-over/lean sensor, so the lean didn't cut it — the wiring moved. NEXT STEPS TO CLOSE IT: (a) Disconnect the battery negative before cutting anything. (b) Pinpoint the exact inch — steady the bundle, wiggle one wire at a time to find which single wire toggles the light, then binary-search it (pinch the midpoint, flex each half, follow the half that flickers; a gentle steady pull while flexing makes the break show up sharper). Breaks usually sit right where a wire enters the back of a connector, or at a hard bend / under an old taped section. (c) Cut out the bad section back to bright clean copper; splice with solder + adhesive-lined heat-shrink (seals against the moisture history) or an adhesive-lined heat-shrink butt connector; leave a little slack so it flexes over a length, not one point, and route clear of the steering-head turn-stops. (d) While it's open, clean the green connector pins (contact cleaner + dielectric grease) — same water exposure, cheap insurance. (e) TEST: continuity-check the repaired wire with the power off, then key on -> headlight solid, then turn the bars lock-to-lock to confirm it stays lit through the full sweep, then check horn + brake light (same feed). Once power is solid, the speedo rebuild moves back to the top. SAFETY while flexing it live: keep any bare wire from touching the frame/engine or it'll pop the main fuse and send you back to square one.

Summer 2025 — the extensive carb + cooling overhaul Paul recalled (his private EXTRACTED.md note had it only as a vague recollection); the OpenAI ChatGPT conversation mine reconstructed the blow-by-blow on 2026-07-22. THE ARC: the bike started hard and would run only on the choke — a classic LEAN condition (clogged pilot / stale gas). Paul cleaned the carburetor and spark plug and installed a NiceCNC extended air/fuel mixture screw, but the old screw had sat ~5.5 turns out and the new one was reset far leaner — it wouldn't catch and backfired. Chasing it richer to ~4 turns out over-corrected into FLOODING: raw fuel leaked from the carb, a flooded cylinder strained the starter (near-hydrolock), and the plug sprayed fuel. ⚠️ SAFETY: while cranking with the plug out to clear the flood, expelled fuel vapor IGNITED — a brief garage flash-fire near the plug (no injury; a hard lesson in not cranking raw fuel near an arcing/ungrounded plug). Separately, the RADIATOR was found visibly damaged on 2025-07-11 — new radiators installed BOTH sides by 2025-07-19, cooling system refilled and bled (an initial trapped air pocket caused smoking + a red temp light until re-bled; the radiator receipt is still unfound — see private service records for the narrowed 7/11–7/19 purchase window). Final loose end: a HIGH IDLE + overheat after the carb work, traced to the idle-speed screw turned in too far (NOT the fuel screw) — backed out to spec. OUTCOME: starts reliably, the start-squeak gone. Fuel-screw baseline for this bike at ~2,900 ft elevation ≈ 1.75–2.5 turns out. Installed + confirmed running: NiceCNC extended mixture screw, DRZ400 air filter, NGK CR8E plug, APE inline fuel filter.

RESOLVED SINCE (Paul-confirmed 2026-07-22): the vacuum petcock now works fine and the fuel-screw washer is back in — the bike is running very well. STILL OPEN: valve clearance has not been confirmed checked.

restoration.item: Fall put-away — oil change + drain the carb
restoration.detail: Autumn 2026, same evening as Blue Thunder. Paul's call 2026-07-27, and it's the better order: fresh oil sits far better over winter than used oil, which carries a little acid and moisture the whole time it sits. So this REPLACES the spring oil change rather than adding to it. Calendar reminder set for the first Saturday of November, recurring yearly — but the date is a placeholder for "too cold to ride," not a deadline; move it to whichever evening the riding actually ends (first frost here averages Oct 17). THE JOB: oil 1.9 US qt with filter (Suzuki 16510-29F00 / HiFlo HF139) — DRY-SUMP, so drain BOTH plugs, crankcase and frame downtube. Drain the float bowl on the BSR36. Check coolant level and condition while you're down there — she's the only one of the two with a cooling system, and it was refilled and bled in 2025. If the evening has room, this is also the natural time to finally check VALVE CLEARANCE — still the one unconfirmed item left over from the 2025 overhaul. BOTH BIKES: fill the tank most of the way with the ethanol-free gas they already run — less air space, less condensation. Battery off the bike, on a tender or somewhere it won't freeze (that's what worked last time). Cover her.

Spring 2027. Battery back on, fresh fuel, prime, check coolant and chain, ride. Should be small if the bowl came out dry in the fall. Fuel-screw baseline for this bike at ~2,900 ft is 1.75–2.5 turns out, if she ever needs re-setting — the 2025 overhaul settled that the hard way.

restoration.detail: Summer 2025 (captured from the ChatGPT mine 2026-07-22; identified as this G22A from an ID-tag photo 2025-09-12 — earlier threads mis-guessed 'G14/G16'). After a family oil change filled it to the dipstick MAX, the cart smoked heavily and sputtered at full throttle — an OVERFILL forced oil through the crankcase breather into the intake/combustion. Draining the carb didn't help (ruled out flooding); the fix was draining + flushing the oil, refilling a measured ~1 qt, and cleaning pooled oil out of the air intake — ran well after (Paul-confirmed). A residual oil-fouled main jet caused a lingering throttle sputter into July. Separately (2025-05-04): left in the rain, ran ~1 mi on low gas then died and wouldn't restart even with starter fluid — no logged resolution, likely subsumed by the June oil work. The 'fill by measure, not to MAX' lesson is now in maintenance.engineOil.

coils.value: Vacuum the condenser coils once or twice a year. On a bottom-freezer LG they sit behind the lower back panel or behind the toe grille at the floor. Dust on the coils is the single most common reason a fridge runs warm and works harder than it needs to.
coils.source: Standard refrigerator maintenance; LG's own care guidance for bottom-freezer models.

temperature.value: 37°F in the refrigerator and 0°F in the freezer are the numbers to hold. A fridge thermometer on a shelf is the cheap way to know — the dial setting is not a reading.
temperature.source: FDA/USDA cold-storage guidance — 40°F or below for the fridge, 0°F for the freezer.

doorSeal.value: Wipe the door gaskets a few times a year and check the seal by closing the door on a dollar bill — if it slides out with no drag, that stretch of gasket is letting warm air in. On a bottom-freezer the drawer gasket is the one that gets missed.
doorSeal.source: Standard appliance practice; the dollar-bill test is the manufacturer-recommended check.

iceMaker.value: It works today, and that is worth keeping. The usual failures are the fill tube freezing over and the inlet valve weakening with age — both show up first as small or hollow cubes rather than as a dead maker. If ice slows down, that is the signal, not the silence.
iceMaker.source: Mom confirmed the ice maker works, 2026-09-01. Failure modes are the documented pattern for LG ice-maker modules.
